text: This Technical Specification has been produced by the O-RAN Alliance. The document is intended to describe best practices for O-RAN Transport Network \(TN\) based on end-to-end packet switching technology. It is recognized that other solutions, not based on packet switching, could be employed or mixed with a packet switching solution. Beyond the solutions described in this document, other packet switching solutions may be adequate for TN and can be considered in future versions of this document.
trace: 3 Scope --> 3.1 Overview
text_preview: This Technical Specification has been produced by the O-RAN Alliance. It describes best practices for O-RAN Transport Network \(TN\) based on end-to-end packet switching technology. Other solutions may be employed or mixed with a packet switching solution, which can be considered in future versions.

trace: 3 Scope --> 3.1 Overview

text: In the context of 3GPP, the TN is referred as a non 3GPP-managed domain that supports connectivity within and between RAN and Core Network CN \(refer to TS 28.530 \[13\]\). Therefore, the TN consolidates the RAN infrastructure by bridging the O-RAN functional split:

text: However, in the context of O-RAN, the O-Cloud can manage certain aspects of RAN connectivity through to the IMS \(for more information refer to WG6 CADS document \[14\]\). This alters the traditional definition of the TN, as certain connectivity aspects are no longer within its scope. Hence, given this shift, we define the TN in O-RAN based on domain and management boundaries, explicitly excluding O-Cloud-managed connectivity. Figure 3.1 presents examples of the interplay between O-CLOUD and TN management domains in RAN connectivity:

text: The TN includes Fronthaul, Midhaul, or Backhaul network \(Figure 3-2\). For the definitions of Fronthaul and Midhaul, authors refer to Open Fronthaul Working Group \(WG4\) CUS specification \[18\]. Backhaul is defined as the TN infrastructure that interconnects the RAN and the Core Network. This document uses the term Xhaul to indicate Fronthaul, Midhaul or Backhaul.

text: This specification defines an architecture for an Open Xhaul transport network based on an end-to- end packet switching architecture that utilizes statistical multiplexing and a hierarchy of packet switching "Transport Node Equipment" \(TNE\) starting at the cell site in the access layer and going to the core layer of the transport network capable of supporting the requirements outlined in the O-RAN WG9 Transport Requirements document \[20\].

text: To allow the operators to offer the most flexibility in designing their RAN infrastructure the Xhaul transport network should utilize the same design paradigm as the transport core, aggregation and pre- aggregation. However, in some instances this may not be an option, so this document identifies other potential access technologies, provides a description and considerations/trade-offs for their usage.

WDM in the access network providing Fronthaul services is covered in a different document \[21\].

text: \- Edge Site Equipment \(E-SE\): the Edge Site Equipment terminates the Attachment Circuit within the O-RAN site to connect to the Transport Network \(e.g. O-CLOUD gateway or a Network Function\).

text_preview: \- Edge Site Equipment \(E-SE\): the Edge Site Equipment terminates the Attachment Circuit within the O-RAN site to connect to the Transport Network \(e.g. O-CLOUD gateway or a Network Function\).

trace: 6 Transport network Reference Design and Requirements --> 6.1 Reference Design and Terminology

text: \- Attachment Circuit \(AC\): the AC is a logical connection that attaches the Edge Site and the Transport Network Equipment. The AC serves as a demarcation between the TN and the O-RAN domains.
trace: 6 Transport network Reference Design and Requirements --> 6.1 Reference Design and Terminology
text_preview: \- Attachment Circuit \(AC\): the AC is a logical connection that attaches the Edge Site and the Transport Network Equipment. The AC serves as a demarcation between the TN and the O-RAN domains.

trace: 6 Transport network Reference Design and Requirements --> 6.1 Reference Design and Terminology

text: \- Bearer: a physical or logical link that connects an Edge Site Equipment to the Transport Network. A bearer can be a wireless or wired link. The bearer refers to the underlying connection for the provisioning of an Attachment Circuit \(e.g. a physical Ethernet connection on which an AC is configured thanks to vlan\). One or multiple attachment circuits may be hosted over the same bearer \(e.g., multiple VLANs on the same bearer realized by a physical link\).
trace: 6 Transport network Reference Design and Requirements --> 6.1 Reference Design and Terminology
text_preview: A bearer is a physical or logical link connecting Edge Site Equipment to the Transport Network, which can be wireless or wired. It's the underlying connection for provisioning an Attachment Circuit, such as a physical Ethernet connection with VLAN configuration. One or multiple attachment circuits may share the same bearer.

trace: 6 Transport network Reference Design and Requirements --> 6.1 Reference Design and Terminology

text:
* O-Cloud and TN Segment: segment of the logical connectivity realized respectively within O-Cloud and Transport Network domains. The O-Cloud segment is optional since the NF may directly attach to the TN via the AC.
  * O-RAN Site: the O-RAN Site refers to a location physical or logical hosting one or more O-RAN components \(e.g., O-RU, O-DU, O-CU\) and may include elements of the O-Cloud.

text: Requirements for the transport architecture can be characterized in following categories:

text_preview: Requirements for the transport architecture can be characterized in following categories:

text:
* 1\. Latency, Frame Loss Ratio and Bandwidth requirements for Fronthaul, Midhaul, and Backhaul.
  * 2\. Operability requirements that include fault and performance management.
  * 3\. Synchronization requirements.
  * 4\. "ITU-T GSTP-TN5G: Transport support of IMT-2020/5G" \[188\] identifies the need for the transport to be multi-service in nature. In addition to mobile services, the infrastructure needs to support fixed line consumer and enterprise services. These services are not explicitly covered in the document, but the architecture must enable L2 or L3 services to be created between any two edge TNEs regardless of relative position to each other in the transport network.
  * 5\. End to end support of 4G/5G mobile infrastructure including Fronthaul / Midhaul / Backhaul.
  * 6\. Concurrent support for RAN deployment scenarios outlined in "ITU-T GSTP-TN5G: Transport support of IMT-2020/5G" \[188\] running from a single cell site location. These shown in Figure 6-3 are:
  * a. Co-located O-CU and O-DU O-RAN split 7.2x from cell site

text:
* O-RAN 7.2x Control and User planes: These interfaces are described in O- RAN.WG4.CUS.0-v09.00: Control, User and Synchronization Plane Specification \[18\]. These interfaces run between the O-RUs and their serving O-DU. Ethernet encapsulation is a mandatory requirement and IP encapsulation is optional and applies if the transmitting and receiving nodes support IP capabilities. In both cases the payload is one or more eCPRI transport headers with respective application data. The latency requirements associated with 7.2x control plane and user plane traffic are very low, and the bandwidth requirements are generally high but vary based on the level of user data traffic being transmitted.
  * O-RAN 7.2x Synchronization plane: This interface is described in O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0- v9.00: Control, User and Synchronization Plane Specification \[18\]. In C-RAN architectures accurate synchronization between the O-DU and O-RUs is required to support "Time Division Duplex" \(TDD\), Carrier Aggregation \(CA\) using multiple O-RUs, MIMO and other processes. text:
* O-RAN 7.2x Management plane: This interface is described in O-RAN.WG4.MP.0-v09.00 Management plane specification\[19\]. Two M-Plane models are defined.
  * o Hierarchical model: In this model, an O-RU is managed by one of more O-DUs. These O-DUs are entirely responsible for sub-ordinate O-RUs, which means the NMS only needs to interact with the O-DU level. In this mode the O-RAN 7.2x M-Plane interface only runs between the O-DU and sub-ordinate O-RUs.
  * o Hybrid model: In this model, an O-RU is managed by one or more NMSs, in addition to the serving O-DU. In this mode the O-RAN 7.2x M-Plane interface runs between the O-RUs, O-DUs and the NMS.

text:
* In this scenario an operator has an existing radio deployed at the cell site and the operator intends to
  * convert these radios to support a C-RAN Fronthaul architecture whilst implementing their 5G RAN
  * infrastructure. In this case it is likely the legacy equipment \(RRH and BBU\) only supports an
  * optical CPRI interfaces. To implement a C-RAN Fronthaul architecture in a packet switched
  * transport network the CPRI needs to be converted to an Ethernet frame at the cell site, transported
  * over the access network as packet and then get converted back to CPRI at the hub for processing
  * from the BBU. In this scenario a component called a RoE mapper is used to perform a CPRI to
  * Ethernet frame conversion at the cell site and an Ethernet frame to CPRI conversion at the location
  * where the BBU is located.
  *   * 7.2.2.1 RoE Mapper transport
  * The design, implementation, management, and interface from the RoE mapper to the legacy
  * equipment is not in the scope of WG-9 but the expectation is the RoE mapper will present either O-
  * RAN 7.2x compliant Ethernet or Ethernet IP packets or IEEE 1914.3 Radio over Ethernet packets
  * \[38\] to the transport network. At this time O-RAN has not defined a CPRI to O-RAN 7.2x
  * conversion capability so implementations out in the market are based on CPRI to Radio Over

text: The structure-agnostic RoE mapper has two main modes of operation:
trace: 7 5G logical connectivity requirements --> 7.2 Non-ORAN Fronthaul

text: • Tunnelling mode or type 0 works as a simple Ethernet tunnel. It does not remove any line coding bits and does not interpret any special characters \(such as K-characters\). If the source data is 8b/10b-encoded, the 10-bit symbols present on the line will be tunnelled by this RoE mapper as 10 bits of data. Similarly, 66-bit symbols will be sent for 64b/66b-encoded data as 66 bits of data. The entire stream is simply packetized.
trace: 7 5G logical connectivity requirements --> 7.2 Non-ORAN Fronthaul
text_preview:
Tunnelling mode (type 0) preserves line coding and special characters, mapping:

- 8b/10b-encoded data to 10-bit symbols
- 64b/66b-encoded data to 66-bit symbols.

trace: 7 5G logical connectivity requirements --> 7.2 Non-ORAN Fronthaul

text: • Line-coding-aware mode or type 1 removes the line coding bits such as for CPRI encoded with 8b/10b or 64b/66b. If the source data is 8b/10b-encoded, the 8-bit symbols present on the line will be tunnelled by this RoE mapper as 8 bits of data. Similarly, if the source data is 64b/66b encoded, the 64-bit symbols present on the line will be tunnelled by this RoE mapper as 64 bits of data. To allow the restoration of the 10-bit or 66-bit symbols at the de- mapper, the RoE mapper/de-mapper must have some awareness of the protocol it is mapping/de-mapping; the locations of the special characters must be known a priori relative to an event that is indicated in the RoE frame.

text: The 5G 3GPP interfaces associated with Backhaul are:
trace: 7 5G logical connectivity requirements -->  --> 7.4 Backhaul logical transport requirements
text_preview: The 5G 3GPP interfaces associated with Backhaul are:

text:
* N1 interface is a logical control plane interface between the mobile core network and the UE. From a physical perspective it flows via the RAN through the Backhaul infrastructure to the AMF. It is a signalling interface between the UE and the AMF.
  * N2 interface supports control plane signalling between RAN and 5G core. It is primarily concerned with connection management, UE context and PDU session management, and UE mobility management. In addition, Non-Access Spectrum \(NAS\) signalling between the UE and the AMF is transported over the N2 connection for that UE. This signalling includes information regarding access control, authentication and authorization, and session management procedures.
  * N4 Interface is the bridge between the control plane and the user plane of the 5GC. It runs between the SMF and the UPF and is responsible for conveying policy rules regarding policy handling, forwarding and usage reporting to the UPF.
  * N3 interface is the user plane interface between the O-CU component of the \(gNB\) and the initial UPF.
  * N9 interface is a user plane interface than runs between two UPFs. \(i.e. an intermediate UPF and the UPF session anchor\).

text: When considering a C-RAN architecture there are both positive and negative impacts. On the positive side, it can increase component efficiency by pooling RAN elements in a centralised location and improve co-ordination between the radio component. On the negative side a C-RAN architecture can significantly increase the bandwidth required if the Fronthaul protocols are traversing the transport network.

  * NR, legacy LTE and legacy UMTS

text: The underlay packet-switching technologies described in this document are based on MPLS and IPv6 with an emphasis on the Segment Routing \(SR\) control and data planes. The overlay service layer uses EVPN and MP-BGP L3VPNs. The IETF is the primary standardization body for these technologies. The key specification of the IETF is the "Request For Comments" \(RFC\). RFCs are labelled with different statuses: Internet Standard, Proposed Standard, Best Current Practice, Experimental, Informational, and Historic. RFCs usually begin as Internet-Drafts written by Individuals, or a small group and are known as individual drafts. Depending on interest an individual draft can be adopted by an IETF Work Group \(WG\) where it is improved and revised by a wider group and can ultimately become an RFC. This process is well defined by the IETF, with guides and considerations for the progression of a document. If the process completes, then the document is published as an RFC by the IETF RFC Editor. If a document does not follow the process or doesn't meet the guidelines outlined, then the drafts will expire and never become an RFC. Depending on subject matter the process of moving from an WG adopted draft to an RFC can

text: As discussed in detail in Section 8, depending on the use case, O-DU function can be placed at the cell site, together with O-RU function, or placed away from the O-RU, at the hub site. The O-DU placement has big influence on the possible physical topology for the access domain of the transport network.

text_preview: The O-DU function's placement affects the access domain's physical topology. It can be placed with or without the O-RU at either the cell site or hub site, significantly influencing the transport network's topology.

text: Open Fronthaul Interface between O-RU and O-DU has very strict latency and timing budgets \(O-RAN.WG9.XTRP-REQ-v01.00 "Xhaul Transport Requirements v01.00", November 2020 \[20\]\). The implication of these requirements on the transport network design is, the number of Transport Network Equipments \(TNEs\) between O-RU and O-DU should be minimized, as each TNE increases the latency and time error.

text: Ring or chain topologies can be used for Fronthaul, providing that latency and timing error budgets required for particular Fronthaul deployment are maintained. For example, designing Fronthaul for standard NR performance \(O-RAN.WG9.XTRP-REQ-v01.00 "Xhaul Transport Requirements v01.00", November 2020 \[20\] Table 3\), mandates maximum 100 s one-way latency between O- RU and O-DU. This latency budget is consumed by the fiber \(~4.9 s/km\), as well as by transit Transport Network Equipments \(~1-20 s per node, depending on hardware capabilities and port speeds\). Assuming 10 s latency per Transport Network Equipment, a chain or ring with 10 Transport Network Equipments would completely consume entire Fronthaul latency budget \(ring might break, so any Fronthaul design must be prepared for link failures not only from traffic rerouting perspective, but as well must take into account increased number of transit network elements, leading to increased latency, under ring failure condition\).

text_preview: Ring or chain topologies can be used for Fronthaul if latency and timing error budgets are maintained. Designing for standard NR performance requires a maximum 100 s one-way latency between O-RU and O-DU, which a 10-Equipment chain would consume.

text: 10 Following delay components contribute to overall Transport Network Equipment delay:
trace: 10.1Packet over fibre --> Table 2 TSN Profile A and Profile B comparison
text_preview: 10 Following delay components contribute to overall Transport Network Equipment delay:

text:
* 12 Frame transmission delay, which is the time taken to transmit the frame at the 13 transmission rate of the port. Since both TSN Profile A and TSN Profile B mandate for 14 Fronthaul data maximum frame size of 2000 bytes, this delay component is equal for 15 Fronthaul data frames with both TSN Profile A and TSN Profile B.
  * 16 Self-queueing delay, which is the delay caused by other frames in the same traffic class as 17 frame to be sent \(i.e. both frames are for example Fronthaul data frames\). The part of the 18 self-queuing delay caused by frames that arrive at more or less the same time from different 19 input ports is referred to as fan-in delay; however, it is simpler to handle fan-in delay as part 20 of the self-queuing delay. Since both TSN Profile A and TSN Profile B mandate that 21 Fronthaul data frames cannot be pre-empted, this delay component is equal for Fronthaul 22 data frames with both TSN Profile A and TSN Profile B.
  * 23 Queuing delay, which is the delay caused by the frame of which transmission already 24 started in an arbitrarily small time before frame X became eligible for transmission, plus the 25 delay caused by queued-up frames from all flows with higher priority than the traffic class 26 of frame X. Since both TSN Profile A and TSN Profile B mandate that Fronthaul data must 27 be prioritized over non-Fronthaul data, in both profiles only single non-Fronthaul frame can 28 contribute to this delay. In case of TSN Profile A, a non-Fronthaul frame size is limited to 29 2,000 bytes \(2,020 bytes including preamble, start of frame delimiter and inter-frame gap\). 30 In case of TSN Profile B, a non-Fronthaul frame can be pre-empted, but at least 155 bytes of 31 pre-empted frame are transmitted due to the characteristics of frame preemption.

text:
* 1\. Ring: This architecture is commonly seen in pre-aggregation and aggregation networks where traffic is being collected and aggregated from the access towards components in the aggregation or transport core. Connectivity between routers is either via direct dark fibre connections or via lambdas derived from a WDM system.
  * 2\. Dual hub and spoke: This architecture is most commonly seen in aggregation and core transport networks but also sometimes in pre-aggregation networks. It is used to collect and aggregate traffic towards common aggregation points. Connectivity between routers is typically via direct dark fibre or via lambdas derived from a WDM system.
  * Note: Hub and spoke architectures are often super-imposed over a physical ring topology using WDM technology.
  * 3\. Mesh: This is architecture is normally seen in transport core networks but can be seen in aggregation networks. It is used when traffic is flowing in an any-to-any fashion. As drive distances increase and connectivity becomes meshier in nature, so there is increasing use of DWDM and ROADM technology to derive the links between routers.

text: The access network uses optical technology with no packet switching transport functionality. Figure 10-9 illustrates a passive WDM Fronthaul design but the same design principle applies regardless of the WDM solution. Each O-RU directly connected to the WDM multiplexer/demultiplexer by a colored optic and an optical cable. At the O-DU side in the central office, the WDM multiplexer/demultiplexer performs wavelength multiplexing/demultiplexing, which realize the one-to-one optical wavelength connection. The WDM solution can be passive, semi active or active.

text: 10.2.2Passive Optical Networks \(PONs\)
trace: 10.1Packet over fibre --> 10.2Alternative physical transport solutions --> 10.2.2Passive Optical Networks \(PONs\)
text_preview: 10.2.2Passive Optical Networks \(PONs\)

text: Passive Optical Networks \(PONs\) are fiber-based point-multipoint access networks, relying on TDM/TDMA for the exchange of traffic between a central Optical Line Termination \(OLT\) and multiple Optical Network Units \(ONUs\). PONs also use WDM for separation of up- and downstream traffic, and for overlaying of multiple different PON technologies over the same fiber infrastructure called Optical Distribution Network \(ODN\). Note that there are two basic flavours of PON;
trace: 10.1Packet over fibre --> 10.2Alternative physical transport solutions --> 10.2.2Passive Optical Networks \(PONs\)
text_preview: Passive Optical Networks (PONs) use TDM/TDMA to exchange traffic between a central OLT and ONUs, with WDM for up- and downstream separation and overlaying multiple PON technologies over an Optical Distribution Network (ODN). There are two basic flavours of PON.

text:
* 1\. Time or Time +Wavelength Division Multiplexing \(TDM or TWDM\) PONs apply point- multipoint connections \(one up/down wavelength pair \(called Channel Pair\) is shared over multiple ONUs\) over a point-multipoint ODN.
  * 2\. Wavelength Division Multiplexing \(WDM\) PONs apply point-point connections between each ONU and the OLT \(one Channel Pair per ONU\) over a point-multipoint ODN.
trace: 10.1Packet over fibre --> 10.2Alternative physical transport solutions --> 10.2.2Passive Optical Networks \(PONs\)
text_preview:
* Time or TWDM PONs: 
  * One up/down wavelength pair (Channel Pair) shared over a point-multipoint ODN.
* WDM PONs:
  * Point-point connections between each ONU and OLT, with one Channel Pair per ONU.

text: WDM PONs are like dedicated point-point links whereas TDM/TWDM PONs have some fundamental characteristics to bear in mind when considering them for mobile Xhaul, described below.

text: TDM/TWDM PONs are standardized technologies \(see \[190\], \[35\], \[36\], \[37\]\) and are characterized by generic capabilities \(independently of the use case\):
trace: 10.1Packet over fibre --> 10.2Alternative physical transport solutions --> 10.2.2Passive Optical Networks \(PONs\)
text_preview: TDM/TWDM PONs are standardized technologies \(see \[190\], \[35\], \[36\], \[37\]\) and are characterized by generic capabilities \(independently of the use case\):

text:
* PON line rates are shared over the ONUs and existing technologies reach 10 Gbit/s per channel \(up to 4x 10 Gbit/s with NG-PON2\), with new variants being developed at 25 Gbit/s and 50 Gbit/s. Note that some fraction is consumed by the technology-specific overheads \(e.g. by parity bits for Forward Error Correction\).
  * Depending on the technology the maximum distance can reach 20 km or 40 km \(or 60 km with a reach extender\), the maximum amount of ONUs per PON port can reach 64 or 128. Note that the reach \(distance\) and scalability \(amount of ONUs per PON ODN\) are a mutual trade-off bound by the optical budget \(many classes of optical budget exist, e.g. Class N1 covers optical losses from 14dB to 29dB\).
  * The max amount of traffic flows per PON port can reach 4k \(independently of physical layer considerations\).
  * The upstream TDMA multiplexing is controlled by a Dynamic Bandwidth Assignment \(DBA\) algorithm in the OLT \(which is equivalent to upstream shaping over the PON segment\). The DBA allocates the bandwidth needs per transport container \(each ONU can have one or multiple transport containers\) and update its assigned bandwidth. The assigned bandwidth is then converted into a burstiness \(rate and size of bursts\). Bandwidth can also be \(partially or fully\) assigned as a fixed value. The upstream latency is influenced by the DBA behaviour, with a trade-off between latency and efficiency \(more frequent bursts means less waiting time between bursts but more overhead\).
  * Protection of \(parts of\) the passive ODN and active OLT equipment by automated switch-over from working to protecting parts of the equipment.
  * Management and configuration of the ONUs. Note that ONUs operate at Layer 2 only \(e.g. for Layer 2 flow classification\). An ONU can be connected to \(or integrated with\) a Layer 3 device like a residential gateway.

text: Note that PON systems are multi-service, hence mixes of different Xhaul flavours can co-exist on the same PON system \(e.g. Midhaul + Backhaul\) and can also co-exist with non-mobile traffic \(e.g. business services\). text: Today's modern cable operators deploy and manage extensive hybrid fiber coaxial \(HFC\) networks. The HFC plant reaches 93% of American households and connects to virtually every building across north America. The data-over-cable service interface specification \(DOCSIS®\) is the protocol designed to work on the HFC network. DOCSIS suite of specifications is standardized and maintained by CableLabs® \[198\]\[199\], and is deployed worldwide. DOCSIS technology has evolved through six generations of progressive refinement. Originally developed for delivering high speed broadband to residential customers, the cable industry has made many advances in the HFC technology, making it a promising option for 5G transport. The HFC plants are already extensively deployed in areas where 5G will be in the most demands, especially in dense urban and suburban environments. Additionally, the HFC plant is active, providing power needed for small cell radios. The cable operators typically have the right of way on the strands where radios can be hung, eliminating the need to obtain permits from government. Leveraging the existing HFC deployments significantly reduces time-to-market and cost of deploying 5G.

text: DOCSIS protocol is a Layer 2 transmission protocol that encapsulates the IEEE 802.3 Ethernet. The technology supports both Layer 2 and Layer 3 services and is aware of both. DOCSIS network is a point-to-multipoint access network, where the transmission of upstream and downstream is controlled by the cable modem termination system \(CMTS\). Figure 10-14 shows a typical HFC plant. The CMTS is typically located in either a headend or a hub, which is connected to the fiber nodes through digital or analog fiber. From there, the communication path traverses through a coax network of zero or more amplifiers to the neighborhoods. The hybrid \(fiber and coax\) network topology is called "N+x", where "N" is the fiber node, where the fiber ends and coax starts, and "x" is the number of amplifiers traversed. The average north American plant is between N+2 and N+5. The smaller the x, the closer the fiber node it is to the neighborhood, the larger the amount of capacity would be available to each customer.

text: Table 4 shows the capabilities of the most recent DOCSIS standards. While DOCSIS 4.0 will provide over 10 Gbps of downstream capacity, even higher rates can be supported. A unique aspect of the DOCSIS technology is its ability to progressively expand downstream and upstream capacities when and where it is needed. Traditionally, the same plant is used to provide video and broadband services. As the cable industry moves away from traditional video delivery, the RF spectrum that is used for video can be reclaimed for broadband. Moreover, as cable operators moves to reduce the "x" in the N+x topology, node segmentation takes place. For every node that is segmented into two, the network capacity essentially doubles.

text: The DOCSIS specification provides a rich set of QoS mechanisms, including traffic classification, queuing, multiple scheduling services, policing, traffic shaping. For UGS/PGS services, there are trade-offs between incurring capacity overhead vs. lowering the latency. text: Cable operators are in the midst of disaggregating the traditional CMTS. The "Distributed Access Architecture" \(DAA\), shown in Figure 10-15, has been specified by CableLabs \[200\] and is being deployed. Replacing the traditional "integrated" CMTS, PHY layer component of the CMTS is being pushed to the fiber node and is called Remote PHY Device \(RPD\), while MAC and upper layers are implemented as DAA Core, and is located in the headend or regional data center. The DAA Core has been architected with the cloud native architecture. The links between the fiber node and the hub are being upgraded to a digital fiber network, with DWDM as a starting point, but some operators may choose to migrate to point-to-point coherent optics. A device called "CTD" is being specified to terminate the fiber from the hub, and is essentially be a Layer 2 switch that provides high-speed Ethernet to the neighborhood. A multitude of services can be provided through the CTD, including 5G Fronthaul, PON, etc, thus achieving a form of transport convergence.

text: Fronthaul is much more difficult to support over the coax portion of the HFC network. Studies have shown that the eCPRI-based Fronthaul transport needs significantly more bandwidth, overhead, and one-way latency in the neighborhood of 250 microseconds between the O-RU and O-DU and between TNEs 100 microseconds. Even with LLX, it will be difficult to reduce the DOCSIS latency to this level. Because of the stringent requirements, Fronthaul is better carried directly over the digital fiber network and over CTD as shown in Figure 10-16.

text: For over 20 years, microwave has been the primary solution for the rapid and cost-effective rollout of mobile Backhaul infrastructure with over 50% of mobile sites worldwide today connected via Microwave \(MW\) or Millimetre Wave \(mmW\) radio links and up to over 90% in some networks. The evolution from 4G towards 5G presents significant challenges to all transport technologies and wireless ones make no exception.

The spectrum that is available for mobile Backhaul ranges from the traditional microwave bands up to the millimetre wave spectrum as illustrated in the Figure 10-17. These bands are allocated for fixed services by the WRC Radio regulations. Their channel plans are detailed by the ITU-R F-series recommendations as well as some regional or national regulatory regimes, such as CEPT. Fixed services spectrum uses authorisations awarded by national

text: MW or mmW links are characterised by their physical capabilities related to the combination of link length, capacity, frequency band and availability, which is independent of their network layer functionalities and use cases. These radio links are usually capable of multiplexing various types of traffic over single radio channel and can be equipped with multiple network interfaces including FE/GbE \(RJ45, SFP\) and CWDM filter support. Various packet functions are also supported as optional features and can be configured by network operators, such as L2 pass through, feature rich L2 switch with ERPS, H-QoS among others enabling carrier grade Ethernet services. MPLS-TP is also supported for layer 2 services, and for timing and synchronisation support includes 1588v2 \(TC, BC\) and SyncE.

text: Data center solutions, connectivity to the Xhaul transport infrastructure and orchestration are not in scope of this version of document. However, it is important to note the critical role Data centers play in 5G, with key components of the 5G architecture running on servers either virtualized, containerized or as bare metal located in data centers. Consequently, operators need to consider how data centers are connected to the Xhaul transport network and how end to end transport services are built that span the DC and the WAN. At a high-level two basic approaches to interconnecting DC to the Xhaul transport network are available.
trace: -->  --> 10.3Data Centers
text_preview: Data center solutions are not in scope. However, data centers host key 5G components on virtualized, containerized, or bare metal servers. text: 10.3.1Complete separation between DC and WAN infrastructure
trace: -->  --> 10.3.1Complete separation between DC and WAN infrastructure

text: This refers to data centers that are discrete from the WAN infrastructure with each domain potentially running different underlay and overlay transport network technologies. The inter- connection between the two domains is via "Data Center Interconnect" \(DCIs\) routers. These routers reside in both the DC and WAN domains and have an awareness of the DC environment on one side and an awareness of the WAN on the other. To provision an end-to-end network service, the data center and the WAN are provisioned separately, using a cross-domain orchestrator to stitch the two separate service environments together.

text: This section outlines a packet switched underlay model based on "Multi-Protocol Label Switching" \(MPLS\). MPLS data plane is based on label switching but has more than one control plane technology. The first, classic approach is based on the control plane developed when MPLS was first conceived in the mid 1990s and utilizes IGPs, BGP-LU, LDP and RSVP. An emerging approach, very appropriate to mobile transport networks, is based on Segment Routing \(SR\) extensions to IGP and BGP, which have been developed since around 2010 and aim to simplify and minimize the number of protocols running in network, as well as reduce the state held on the TNEs. This document describes scalable, multi-domain Xhaul transport architecture that can involve domains with different MPLS control plane technologies \(classic: LDP, RSVP, BGP-LU, as well as emerging: SR, SR with Flex-Algo, or SR-TE\), in order to support both brownfield \(extending existing mobile transport network using classic control plane with additional domains using new, emerging SR control plane\) and greenfield \(building new Xhaul transport network\) deployment use cases. However, in order to avoid duplications with BBF technical reports documenting classic MPLS control plane in mobile transport network designs, and to keep the size of this document within reasonable limits, this document puts more focus on the new, emerging control plane based on SR.

A scalable, multi-domain Xhaul transport architecture is described, involving domains with different MPLS control plane technologies, including classic and emerging Segment Routing approaches since 2010.

text:
* 1\. Each routing domain has an IGP for internal connectivity.
  * 2\. Each routing domain has a protocol for distributing label information. It could be SR extension to an IGP, or could be as well legacy protocol like RSVP or LDP. Architecture supporting legacy MPLS transports \(LDP and/or RSVP\) is especially important in brown-field deployments, with legacy MPLS transport already in place.
  * 3\. Mechanisms to calculate Traffic Engineered paths within a routing domain. Depending on scale, TE paths can be calculated on the transport devices themselves \(distributed constrained shortest path first – D-CSPF – calculation\), calculation can be off-loaded from less powerful transport devices to more powerful transport devices \(on-box PCE\), or even dedicated servers could be deployed \(off-box PCE\). The diagram shows a distributed "Path Computation Element" \(PCE\) layer with "Path Computation Element Protocol" PCEP running between the edge nodes and the PCE
  * 4\. Mechanism to establish end-to-end MPLS LSPs between IGP domains. To achieve highly scalable architecture, two mechanism could be considered: Seamless MPLS Architecture, or a controller-based Architecture. Both architectures are described in more details in Section 11.5.
  * 5\. Mechanism to convey topology and network state information from the network to the PCE and other management elements. BGP Link State \(BGP-LS\) and Telemetry feeds are recommended tools to fulfil this requirement.

text:
* The following section outlines the control plane requirements for SR/MPLS environment.
  * 11.4.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SR/MPLS
  * The distribution of labels, rapid convergence and distribution of traffic engineering information and
  * optional calculation of TE optimized transport planes in a single SR domain is done by a link-state
  * IGP, in the form of either IS-IS or ISPF, with suitable SR enhancements. This document separately
  * outlines the requirements for IS-IS and OSPF with support for TiLFA for fast convergence and
  * optional support for flex-algorithm for the creation of multiple transport planes optimised for
  * different criteria and potentially using different topologies.

text: For each destination in the network, TI-LFA pre-installs a backup forwarding entry for each protected destination ready to be activated upon detection of the failure of a link used to reach the destination. TI-LFA provides protection in the event of any one of the following: single link failure, single node failure, or single SRLG failure. In link failure mode, the destination is protected assuming the failure of the link. In node protection mode, the destination is protected assuming that the neighbor connected to the primary link has failed. In SRLG protecting mode, the destination is protected assuming that a configured set of links sharing fate with the primary link has failed \(e.g. a linecard or a set of links sharing a common transmission pipe\). The mechanics of the TiLFA in an SR/MPLS environment at failure is shown in Figure 11-3 and upon convergence in Figure 11-4. One of the key advantages of TiLFA over some other fast convergence mechanisms, not well illustrated in the example below, is that the TiLFA backup path is the same as the post convergence path, thus minimising micro-loops that can occur as IGPs converge.
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.4SR/MPLS control plane
text_preview:
TI-LFA pre-installs backup forwarding entries for protected destinations upon link failure detection. It protects against:

- Single link failure
- Node failure (primary neighbor)
- SRLG failure (configured set of links sharing fate)

Protection is based on post-convergence paths to minimize micro-loops during IGPs convergence.

text: 11.4.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.4SR/MPLS control plane --> 11.4.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm
text_preview: 11.4.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm

text: In the SR/MPLS underlay design outlined in this document Flexible Algorithm can be used to within an IGP domain to provide an IGP based traffic engineering facility. Flexible-Algorithm is an IGP based traffic engineering technique that permits multiple forwarding tables to be created in the IGP based on operator programmed criteria. It is a simple, automatic way, in which a packet switched transport network can be traffic engineered, using only the IGP, to create different transport planes designed to meet specific operator defined criteria.

text: Standard ISIS and OSPF use the IGP metric on links and the "Shortest Path First" \(SPF\) algorithm to calculate the "best" path between an ingress and egress point in the network. For many services this approach is sufficient, however this approach cannot, for example, take into account real-time link latency, utilization, packet loss and whether an ECMP path shares links using the same underlying fibre ducts.
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.4SR/MPLS control plane --> 11.4.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm
text_preview: Standard ISIS and OSPF use IGP metric on links with "Shortest Path First" (SPF) algorithm to find best paths between ingress and egress points in the network. However, this approach can't account for real-time link latency, utilization, packet loss, or shared fibre ducts.

This is illustrated in Figure 11-5.

text: 11.4.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.4SR/MPLS control plane --> 11.4.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm
text_preview: 11.4.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm

text:
* IGP Flexible-Algorithm is described in section 11.4.1.2. It is an IGP based traffic engineering
  * technique that permits multiple logical topologies to be created in an IGP domain based on operator
  * programmed criteria. When used in a single IGP routing domain the IGP calculates and maintains
  * the path. The ingress node simply needs to address the packet to the MPLS label associated with the
  * flexible algorithm. This removes the need for a head-end or centralised PCE path computation
  * element and also keeps SID list contained in the label stack to a minimum.
  * This works in a single IGP domain but depending on area border router and autonomous system
  * border router capabilities can be supported in multi-domain environments based on redistribution.
  * For flex-algo requirements for SR/MPLS, see section 11.4.1.3 and 11.4.1.4.

text_preview: IGP Flexible-Algorithm is an IGP-based traffic engineering technique that creates multiple logical topologies based on operator-programmed criteria. It eliminates head-end path computation elements, working in single-domain environments and supporting multi-domains through redistribution.

text: 11.5Scaling the MPLS infrastructure
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5Scaling the MPLS infrastructure

text:
* In order to provide communication between two MPLS TNEs, end-to-end MPLS LSPs must be
  * available between the TNEs. This implies, that unique MPLS label towards the Transport Network
  * Equipment, which possibly resides in different routing domain, must be available. In highly scaled
  * environment the number of potential next-hops can be high, therefore care must be taken to ensure
  * that resources, especially forwarding plane resources, are utilized in an efficient way, while
  * providing end-to-end MPLS connectivity.
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5Scaling the MPLS infrastructure
text_preview:
To provide communication between two MPLS TNEs, end-to-end MPLS LSPs must be available.
This requires a unique MPLS label towards Transport Network Equipment, even if in different routing domains.
In highly scaled environments, efficient resource utilization is crucial to ensure end-to-end MPLS connectivity.

text:
* While the requirement for having unique label per remote Transport Network Equipment increases
  * the pressure on scaling, the benefit of unique label is faster detection of remote Transport Network
  * Equipment failure, resulting from unique underlay prefix/label withdrawal. For architectures, which
  * can use prefix summarization for remote Transport Network Equipment reachability, like for
  * example SRv6 architecture discussed in Section 12, such capability is missing, since remote
  * Transport Network Equipment failure does not influence underlay summary prefix state.
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5Scaling the MPLS infrastructure
text_preview:
While scaling increases, unique labels offer faster detection of remote Transport Network Equipment failures.
This benefit is lost for architectures using prefix summarization, like SRv6, where underlay prefix/label withdrawal doesn't affect reachability.

text: BGP-LU operation can be further optimized for enhanced scaling:
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5.1Seamless MPLS architecture
text_preview: BGP-LU operation can be further optimized for enhanced scaling:

text:
* BGP-LU prefixes \(loopbacks of remote TNE\) are not installed in the forwarding table \(FIB\) they are just installed in the routing table \(RIB\), which consumes only control plane resources. On typical transport device, control plane resources scale better than forwarding plane resources 
  * Service NLRIs \(L3VPN, EVPN\) are automatically filtered on route reflectors \(not shown in Figure 11-6, for diagram simplicity\), and distributed only to the TNEs requiring specific service prefixes. This is achieved with constrained route distribution.
  * Only these automatically filtered service NLRIs are installed in the forwarding plane, using the BGP-LU transport label of the required BGP-LU prefix \(remote TNE loopback\). Therefore, usage of forwarding plane resources is highly minimized.
  * Further optimization of control plane resources is possible, where TNE \(PE\) requests from route reflector only limited set of BGP-LU prefixes. This can be achieved with outbound route filtering \(ORF\) of BGP-LU prefixes with ORF filter automatically generated to allow only BGP-LU prefixes required to resolve protocol next-hops of accepted \(filtered with constrained route distribution mechanism\) service NLRIs.
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5.1Seamless MPLS architecture
text_preview: BGP-LU prefixes for remote TNE loopbacks consume control plane resources, impacting transport devices more than forwarding planes. Service NLRIs are filtered on route reflectors and distributed to required TNEs using constrained route distribution. Limiting TNE PE requests through outbound route filtering (ORF) can optimize this process.

text: With Seamless MPLS architecture, ingress PE uses recursive next-hop resolution, where service NLRI received from remote PE is resolved over BGP protocol next-hop \(BGP-LU loopback of remote PE\), which in turn is resolved over local intra-domain MPLS tunnel \(SR/SR-TE or legacy RSVP/LDP\).
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5.1Seamless MPLS architecture
text_preview: With Seamless MPLS architecture, ingress PE uses recursive next-hop resolution. Service NLRI received from remote PE is resolved via BGP protocol next-hop, which is then resolved over a local intra-domain MPLS tunnel (SR/SR-TE or legacy RSVP/LDP).

text: In addition to the "Seamless MPLS" approach which is an infrastructure-based scaling technique, an external controller in the form of a distributed "Path Computational Element" \(PCE\) could be used for scaling across multiple MPLS domains. The approach aims to simplify the underlying infrastructure by reducing interactions between domains at the infrastructure level and delegating cross domain path determination to a distributed PCE component.

In scenarios where the headend is not able to resolve the next-hop locally, it may rely on PCE to provide an End-to-End Path when requested. The headend communicates with the PCE using Path Computation Element Protocol \(PCEP\). This mechanism can helps save resources on CSR's contributing to overall Xhaul Network scale.

text_preview: 11.5.2.1 Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale

text: Forwarding Adjacency abstracting the path between domain boundary routers is one of the ways to optimize and scale a controller based Xhaul architecture. Forwarding Adjacency architecture is based on following architectural concepts:
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5.1Seamless MPLS architecture --> 11.5.2.1 Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale
text_preview: Forwarding Adjacency abstracting the path between domain boundary routers is one of the ways to optimize and scale a controller based Xhaul architecture. Forwarding Adjacency architecture is based on following architectural concepts:

text:
* Transport network is divided into multiple smaller routing domains. Routing domains can be represented by separate BGP autonomous systems, or separate IGP domains \(areas\). Or, combination of BGP autonomous systems and IGP areas, where BGP autonomous systems are further divided with IGP areas.
  * The size of each routing domain might vary, but must be chosen in such a way, that even the weakest transport device in given routing domain can participate in intra-domain routing and intra-domain MPLS path \(SR, SR-TE, Flex-Algo, RSVP, LDP\) establishment without any scaling concerns
  * Head-end router \(border router\) of intra-domain LSP advertises the intra-domain LSP \(of any kind, i.e. SR, SR-TE, Flex-Algo, RSVP, LDP\) as standard link in BGP Link State \(LS\) topology database, with attributes similar to standard link, like for example SR Adjacency-SID, administrative group \(link color, link affinity\), SRLG, etc. IGP forwarding adjacency is established \(RFC 4206\) between domain border routers creating abstracted topology of the routing domain.
  * BGP-LS \(RFC 8571\) is used to distribute abstracted topology. Given the fact that only border routers, and only abstracted forwarding adjacency links between these border routers are exported, the size of the topology database exported via BGP-LS is considerably smaller. BGP-LS distribution can happen in two way, depending on the overall network scale
  * o BGP-LS topology is exchanged between routers in different routing domains
  * o BGP-LS topology is exchanged between PCEs in distributed PCE layer
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5.1Seamless MPLS architecture --> 11.5.2.1 Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale
text_preview: a transport network is divided into smaller routing domains , represented by separate bgp autonomous systems or igp areas . each domain accommodates weak devices for intra - domain routing and mpls path establishment . the head - end router advertises its lsp as a standard link in bgp link state topology database with attributes like sr adjacency -

text: The first approach is more suitable for small to medium scale deployments. In this approach, any Transport Network Equipment has the detailed topology visibility of the local routing domain, and abstracted \(with Forwarding Adjacencies advertised as links in BGP-LS\) visibility of the remote routing domains. This significantly reduces the topology database stored on the Transport Network Equipments, therefore, in small/medium deployments PCE might not be necessary.
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5.1Seamless MPLS architecture --> 11.5.2.1 Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale
text_preview: For small to medium scale deployments, Transport Network Equipment has detailed local topology and abstracted remote routing domain visibility via Forwarding Adjacencies advertised as links in BGP-LS. This reduces the topology database on equipment, making PCE less necessary.

text: The headend PE, based on the full topology database \(detailed topology from local routing domain + topology abstracted with links representing forwarding adjacencies from remote routing domains\), performs calculation of end-to-end SR-TE paths \(local constrained shortest path first – CSPF – calculation\). Each forwarding adjacency is represented in the resulting SR-TE label stack as single Adjacency-SID associated with given forwarding adjacency, regardless of the underlying
trace: 11 Packet-switched underlay network – MPLS based --> 11.5.1Seamless MPLS architecture --> 11.5.2.1 Forwarding Adjacency architecture for cross domain scale
text_preview: The headend PE uses a full topology database to calculate end-to-end SR-TE paths using CSPF. Each forwarding adjacency is represented as a single Adjacency-SID in the resulting label stack, regardless of the underlying routing domain.

text: As further scaling optimization of this architecture, ingress PEs \(typically cell site routers, with limited control plane resources required for efficient end-to-end path computation\) can be off- loaded from end-to-end path computation. Distributed PCEs \(Path Computation Elements\) can be placed on more powerful transport devices \(for example pre-aggregation or aggregation routers\), or containerized/virtualized PCE function can be placed in the distributed telco cloud environment to execute end-to-end path computation duties over simplified \(via forwarding adjacencies\) full network topology. In this scenario, ingress PE requests from PCE on demand path computation for unresolved next-hops, as outlined in Figure 11-11.

text: As mentioned earlier, a controller-based architecture make use of the PCE to provides the SID list to the headend for an end-to-end path across multiple domains. If no constraints are imposed on the traffic, the SID list would consist of Area Border Routers Prefix SIDs as next hop. Traffic within the domain will use IGP to get to the next hop while utilizing well established IGP routing mechanism such as Equal Cost Multi Path \(ECMP\), metric based best path etc. At the ABR, the top most SID is popped and the new next hop SID/Label is exposed, starting the routing within the next IGP are or domain. The process is repeated until traffic reaches its destination. Figure 11-12 shows such behaviour between IGP Domain 0,1 and 2.

text: There may be scenarios where more explicit path considerations and constraints could be required, such as using low latency path or inclusion/exclusion of certain links or node. In those scenarios, rather than provide a SID list that encompasses every link/node through the path, mechanisms such as Flex Algo could be used to optimize the SID list on the head end. Figure 11-13 shows a scenario with latency and link/node constraints across the path. In this case operator may use Flex-Algo within a domain and use the PCE controller to provide SID list to the headend accordingly. Notice while the SID depth is no different from the earlier scenario Figure 11-13\) and while it still only contain prefix-SIDs of ABR as next hop label, the SID's now refer to the node's Flex-Algo Prefix SID, instead of default algo SID. Due to this, the traffic behavior is also different and the next Hop SID automatically uses the desired constraints-based path.

text: In scenarios where an operator is unable or unwilling to use Flex-Algo for SID list optimization, an SRTE Binding SID \(BSID\) could be used. A Binding SID is a fundamental component of Segment Routing network that may be used to provide SID and network scaling. A BSID is a SID that is associated with an SRTE policy's active path and is a representation of an End-to-End candidate path. BSIDs could be used to provide additional scale by using nested SRTE policies across domains. The PCE instead of providing a full path through multiple domains, may provide the headend with a path within its own domain and a BSID corresponding to the next domain. When, exposed at the domain boundaries, the BSID gets translated into another set of SID List, providing extensibility and scalability throughout the topology. This process is shown in Figure 11-14.

text: This document presents two packet switched underlay technologies, the first based on MPLS contained in section 11 and the second based on SRv6 contained in this section \(section 12\). An operator wishing to implement the transport architecture outlined in this document will need to select one of the two and implement the requirements outlined in the associated section. It should be noted that other transport architectures are potentially available but not covered in this revision of the document. This section outlines a packet switched underlay model based on SRv6.

  * 5G infrastructure. In contrast, the services infrastructure runs on-top of the underlay/fabric of the
  * transport network and supports the different components of the 5G infrastructure \(Fronthaul,
  * Midhaul, Backhaul\).
  * This chapter is specific to an SRv6 underlay/fabric, its data plane, control plane and how to scale it.
  * Although there are some similarities with an SR-MPLS environment, in terms of architecture, there

text: The SRv6 control plane refers to routing and path control within the SRv6 underlay/fabric. This infrastructure can extend to customer devices or stop at a Provider Edge \(PE\) function. Its role can be summarised as learning the topology, calculation, and implementation of dynamic and explicit routes across the SRv6 infrastructure and providing rapid protection and repair mechanisms. In a packet switched transport network consisting of a large number of routers, a mix of WAN and data centers components, the need to support traffic engineering, the underlay control plane is a typically a collection of independent routing domains that interact in a collaborate fashion.

It learns topology, calculates dynamic routes, and implements rapid protection mechanisms. The underlay is a collection of independent routing domains that collaborate in a coordinated manner.

text:
* 1\. Each routing domain has an IGP for internal connectivity.
  * 2\. Mechanisms to calculate SR policies or Traffic Engineer paths and convey them to the source nodes. Figure 12-1 shows a distributed "Path Computation Element" \(PCE\), with "Path Computation Element Protocol" \(PCEP\) running between the edge nodes and the PCE but there are other network-based mechanisms to calculate SR policies such as Flex-algo running in the IGP or head-end calculated paths.
  * 3\. Mechanisms to convey routing between IGP domains. This could be provided by summarization and redistribution, E-BGP between AS boundaries or via a multi-domain "Path Computation Element" \(PCE\). One of the key differences between an MPLS and IPv6 based underlay is that IPv6 enables address summarization within routing domains and also between routing domains. This makes an IPv6 based underlay network more scalable and less complex than a corresponding MPLS solution.
  * 4\. Mechanisms to convey topology and network state information from the network to the PCE and other central management elements. BGP Link State \(BGP-LS\) and Telemetry feeds are recommended tools to fulfil this requirement.

text: 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2SRv6 control plane --> 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6
text_preview: 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6

text: SRv6 requires at least one IPv6 IGP per routing domain or autonomous system. There are two IGPs that support SRv6; ISIS for IPv6 or OSPFv3. They are both link-state protocols and have similar capabilities but there are operational differences which is beyond the scope of this document.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2SRv6 control plane --> 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6
text_preview: SRv6 requires at least one IPv6 IGP per routing domain or autonomous system. There are two IGPs that support SRv6; ISIS for IPv6 or OSPFv3. They are both link-state protocols and have similar capabilities but there are operational differences which is beyond the scope of this document.

text: The IGP provides internal connectivity within a routing domain. The size of a routing domain is determined by technical, operational and organizational considerations, such as protocol scalability and spans of control. In large networks, such as a 5G infrastructure, extending from the access to the transport core, it is very common to see multiple autonomous systems, IGPs and segmentation within the IGPs.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2SRv6 control plane --> 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6
text_preview: The IGP provides internal connectivity within a routing domain, influenced by technical, operational, and organizational factors such as protocol scalability and control spans. In large networks, like 5G infrastructures, it's common to see multiple autonomous systems, IGPs, and segmentation within them.

text: In an SRv6 environment the IGP is responsible for distributing node, prefix and SID information to all nodes within the routing domain and for calculating the forward tables between these nodes. Optionally it can provide fast convergence mechanisms and distribute traffic engineering attributes within the domain and build multiple transport planes. Both IS-IS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 have facilities to create a hierarchical routing structure within a routing domain using levels and areas respectively. They also have the facility to bring external routing information into a routing domain and push routing information into other routing domains using route redistribution.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2SRv6 control plane --> 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6
text_preview: In an SRv6 environment, IGP distributes node, prefix, and SID info to all nodes within the routing domain, calculating forward tables and providing fast convergence mechanisms. Both IS-IS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 support hierarchical routing structures using levels and areas with route redistribution capabilities.

text: Note: There are other techniques to achieve route re-distribution between routing domains, such as BGP and centralised SDN controllers.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2SRv6 control plane --> 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6
text_preview: Note: There are other techniques to achieve route re-distribution between routing domains, such as BGP and centralised SDN controllers.

text:
* Note: When looking at SRv6 IGP requirements, there are sets of requirements for ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3. Operators need to follow the requirements associated with IGPs they are using within their network infrastructure.
  * 12.2.1.1 Topology Independent Loop Free Alternative \(TiLFA\)
  * In the SRv6 underlay design outlined in this document TiLFA can be used to achieve fast IGP convergence in the event of a network failure. Topology Independent Loop Free Alternative as
  * defined "Topology Independent Fast Reroute" using Segment Routing \[174\] is an IGP capability
  * supported by Segment Routing that provides a local repair mechanism that achieves 100% coverage
  * within a routing domain against links, nodes and SRLGs failures with convergence times, once
  * failure detection has occurred, H/W dependent but typically less than 50ms.

When using SRv6 IGP requirements, operators must follow their network's IGPs.
TiLFA provides fast IGP convergence in case of a failure, supporting 100% coverage against link, node, and SRLG failures with convergence times < 50ms.

text: For each destination in the network, TI-LFA pre-installs a backup forwarding entry for each protected destination ready to be activated upon detection of the failure of a link used to reach the destination. TI-LFA provides protection in the event of any one of the following: single link failure, single node failure, or single SRLG failure. In link failure mode, the destination is protected assuming the failure of the link. In node protection mode, the destination is protected assuming that the neighbor connected to the primary link has failed. In SRLG protecting mode, the destination is protected assuming that a configured set of links sharing fate with the primary link has failed \(e.g. a linecard or a set of links sharing a common transmission pipe\). The mechanics of the TiLFA for SRv6 at failure is shown in Figure 12-2 and upon convergence in Figure 12-3. One of the key advantages of TiLFA over some other fast convergence mechanisms, not well illustrated in the example below, is that the TiLFA backup path is the same as the post convergence path, thus minimising micro-loops that can occur as IGPs converge.

text: 12.2.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2SRv6 control plane --> 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6
text_preview: 12.2.1.2 IGP Flexible-Algorithm

text: IGP Flexible-Algorithm is an IGP based traffic engineering technique that permits multiple forwarding tables to be created in the IGP based on operator programmed criteria. It is a simple, automatic way, in which a packet switched transport network can be traffic engineered, using only the IGP, to create different transport planes designed to meet specific operator defined criteria. Standard ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 use the IGP metric on links and the "Shortest Path First" \(SPF\) algorithm to calculate the "best" path between an ingress and egress point in the network. For many services this approach is sufficient, however this approach cannot, for example, take into account real-time link latency, utilization, packet loss and whether an ECMP path shares links using the same underlying fibre ducts.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2SRv6 control plane --> 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6
text_preview: IGP Flexible-Algorithm creates multiple forwarding tables based on operator-programmed criteria. It's a simple way to traffic engineer packet-switched networks using IGP, creating transport planes for specific criteria. Unlike SPF algorithms used in ISIS and OSPFv3, it can't account for real-time link latency or utilization.

trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2SRv6 control plane --> 12.2.1Interior Gateway Protocol \(IGP\) for SRv6

text: IGP Flex-Algo, defined in RFC 9350 \[160\] is an IGP based Segment Routing traffic engineering capability, that enables an operator to define their own custom algorithm, based on a wide range of variables including: link latency, packet loss, bandwidth, affinity and shared risk link groups \(SRLG\), to achieve a specific forwarding aim. This is illustrated in Figure 12-4.

text: 12.2.2SRv6 Traffic Engineering
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2SRv6 Traffic Engineering
text_preview: 12.2.2SRv6 Traffic Engineering

trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2SRv6 Traffic Engineering

text:
* SRv6 supports two forms of SR policies or SR Traffic Engineering. Both solutions rely on the IGP to gather and convey topological and resource information around the network and optionally to a
  * Path Computation Element \(PCE\) optimized for SR via BGP-LS.
  * 12.2.2.1 Segment Routing Traffic Engineering \(SR-TE\)
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2SRv6 Traffic Engineering
text_preview:
* SRv6 supports two forms of SR policies or SR Traffic Engineering, both relying on IGP to gather and convey topological information around the network. Solutions include:
  * Path Computation Element (PCE) optimized for SR via BGP-LS.
  * Segment Routing Traffic Engineering (SR-TE).

text: The SR policy consists of a list of SIDs the packet needs to traverse and is programmed into the packet on the source node. The SID list can consist of a mix of prefix and adjacency SIDs. In SR this form of TE allows a path to be:
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2SRv6 Traffic Engineering
text_preview: The SR policy consists of a list of SIDs the packet needs to traverse and is programmed into the packet on the source node. The SID list can consist of a mix of prefix and adjacency SIDs. In SR this form of TE allows a path to be:

text:
* 1\. Loosely source routed where some intermediate points, but not all, are specified between the ingress and egress node. Paths between these intermediate points typically use the shortest path, ECMP based routing determined by the IGP.
  * 2\. Explicitly source routed where all intermediate points and even links are specified between the ingress and egress nodes.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2SRv6 Traffic Engineering
text_preview:
*   Loosely source routed: Intermediate points (not all) are specified between ingress and egress node, using shortest path ECMP routing determined by IGP.
*   Explicitly source routed: All intermediate points and links are specified between ingress and egress nodes.

trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2SRv6 Traffic Engineering

text: In all cases, topology information and live network status within a routing domain is distributed within a routing domain by the IGP with suitable extensions. In single routing domain environments path computation can be performed either by individual head-end routers or via a centralised "SR Path Computational Element" \(SR-PCE\). In multi-domain routing environments, then path computation generally occurs on a "centralised SR-PCE" component that has topology information for all domains being traversed. This function can be a standalone entity or be integrated into strategically placed TNEs. This form of traffic engineering can support loose and explicitly routed paths, low-latency paths, bandwidth-guaranteed paths, and disjoint paths. Precise TE capability

Multi-domain environments rely on centralized SR-PCE components with combined topology info for all traversed domains, supporting loose, low-latency paths.

text: 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm
text_preview: 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm

text: IGP Flexible-Algorithm is described in section 12.2.1.2. It is an IGP based traffic engineering technique that permits multiple logical topologies to be created in an IGP domain based on operator programmed criteria. When used in a single IGP routing domain the IGP calculates and maintains the path. The ingress node simply needs to address the packet to the "locator-block" associated with the flexible algorithm. This removes the need for a head-end or centralised PCE path computation element and also keeps SID list to a minimum.

text: 12.2.3Inter-domain connectivity
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3Inter-domain connectivity
text_preview: 12.2.3Inter-domain connectivity

text:
* In a large packet-switched transport network the underlay infrastructure will need to be sub-divided
  * into multiple routing domains. These routing domains can be within an autonomous system, at the
  * IGP level, or between autonomous systems. One motivation is IGP scalability, but other reasons
  * include fault isolation between domains and organizational, for example different groups run the
  * DC and WAN infrastructures. However, even though the infrastructure is divided, connectivity
  * between routers in different routing domains is still required to build end to end services, therefore
  * the underlay infrastructure needs mechanisms to enable inter-domain connectivity and services to
  * be built inter-domain. In an SRv6 environment, potential mechanisms for interchanging routing
  * between domains include:
  *   * 1\. IGP based hierarchy
  * 2\. Inter-domain IGP redistribution
  * 3\. Inter AS BGP
  * 4\. Controller based
  *

text: 12.2.3.1 IGP based hierarchy
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3.1 IGP based hierarchy
text_preview: 12.2.3.1 IGP based hierarchy

text:
* Both ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 have the concept of routing hierarchy in their basic designs. In an
  * SRv6 environment, route summarization or injection of a default route between IS-IS levels or
  * OSPFv3 areas is sufficient to enable EVPN or L3VPNs services to be built over an SRv6
  * hierarchical IGP infrastructure.
  *
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3.1 IGP based hierarchy
text_preview: In SRv6, routing hierarchy enables EVPN/L3VPNs via route summarization or default route injection between IS-IS levels or OSPFv3 areas, supporting a hierarchical IGP infrastructure.

text: 12.2.3.2 Inter-domain IGP redistribution
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3.2 Inter-domain IGP redistribution
text_preview: 12.2.3.2 Inter-domain IGP redistribution

text:
* One or more routers are located on the boundary between two or more IGP routing domains. These
  * routers run multiple IGP instances, so have routing awareness of all the IGPs they participate in.
  * Routing information is mutually re-distributed between the IGP protocols allowing reachability
  * between the domains. This redistribution can be in the form of full routing, summarised routes or
  * even default routes. The choice is dependent on the level of awareness required between domains.
  *   * See Figure 12-5 for more detail. IGP route re-distribution in both IS-IS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 is a
  * common capability.
  *
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3.2 Inter-domain IGP redistribution
text_preview: Routers at domain boundaries run multiple IGP instances, gaining routing awareness of all participating IGPs. Routing information is redistributed between protocols, allowing reachability between domains. Redistribution can be full, summarized, or default routes, depending on required awareness.

text: 12.2.3.3 Inter-AS BGP based routing
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3.3 Inter-AS BGP based routing
text_preview: 12.2.3.3 Inter-AS BGP based routing

* A router in each autonomous system exchanges routing information using BGP-4 supporting the
  * IPv6 address family. It should be noted that this scheme provides better separation than inter-
  * domain IGP redistribution but typically requires separate routers in each autonomous system.
  * See Figure 12-6 for more detail.
  *

trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3.4 Controller based path calculation
text_preview: 12.2.3.4 Controller based path calculation

text:

  * Instead, each routing domain provides its topology to an SR Path Computation Element \(SR-PCE\),
  * which is a central SDN control element responsible for determining and finding routes to a
  * destination node on behalf of a source node. Although the SR-PCE is logically a central component,
  * for scale and resiliency reasons it can consist of multiple individual entities distributed around and

text: A SR-PCE function in an SRv6 underlay transport network has three main functions.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3.4 Controller based path calculation
text_preview: A SR-PCE function in an SRv6 underlay transport network has three main functions.

text:
* 1\. Gather data about the topology of the overall SRv6 network underlay. Several options exist:
  * a. The SR-PCE participates in the IGP domains and directly collects each domains IGP link-state database.
  * b. Use BGP Link-State \(BGP-LS\) with appropriate extensions for SRv6 to collect the IGP's link-state database from each routing domain. This is done through one or more BGP session between the SR-PCE and a TNE in each routing domain participating in the domain's IGP. The TNEs retrieve information from the IGP LSDB and distribute it to the controller using the BGP link-state address family.
  * 2\. Communications between the PCE and PCC \(path computation client\) which is the headend TNE. In this document it is assumed to PCEP \(path computation Element Protocol\) is used as the communication mechanism between the source TNE and the SR-PCE.
  * 3\. Path computation. The PCE uses information gathered from the various domains to compute an SR policy consisting of a SID list which packets using the SR policy will traverse. This SID list can be a loosely sourced routed or explicitly source routed.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.2.2.2 IGP Flexible Algorithm --> 12.2.3.4 Controller based path calculation
text_preview:
Gather data on SRv6 network topology:

* Use BGP-LS with SRv6 extensions to collect IGP link-state databases.
* TNE retrieves info, distributes it to controller using BGP link-state address family.
* PCE and headend (TNE) communicate via PCEP.

text: 12.3Scaling an SRv6 underlay infrastructure
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.3Scaling an SRv6 underlay infrastructure
text_preview: 12.3Scaling an SRv6 underlay infrastructure

text: Scaling is one of the key challenges in building a packet switched infrastructure supporting 5G services. Communications and support of L2 and L3 VPN services between two SRv6 TNEs relies entirely on IP routing mechanisms on the underlay transport fabric. In SRv6 this is based on longest IP prefix matching and forwarding, so TNEs can support routing and forwarding based on full IPv6 host routes, summarized IPv6 routes or default routing or a combination, derived from dynamic routing protocols or statically defined. Further, different TNEs in the end to end path can use different levels of route summarization appropriate to their position in the network and their computation, memory and NPU/ASIC resources.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.3Scaling an SRv6 underlay infrastructure
text_preview: Scaling is a key challenge in 5G packet switching infrastructure. SRv6 uses IP routing mechanisms for L2 and L3 VPN services between two TNEs, employing longest prefix matching and forwarding. Different TNEs use varying levels of route summarization based on network position and resources.

text: 12.3.1Route summarization and redistribution
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.3Scaling an SRv6 underlay infrastructure --> 12.3.1Route summarization and redistribution
text_preview: 12.3.1Route summarization and redistribution

text:
* Summarization within ISIS for IPv6 and OSPFv3 is part of the base protocol capability and can
  * occur between levels in IS-IS for IPv6 and between areas in OSPFv3 using "Area Border Routers"
  * \(ABRs\). Summarization is also a common capability when redistributing routes between different
  * routing domains and is also supported between Autonomous Systems using BGP-4 between
  * "Autonomous System Border Routers" \(ASBRs\). This is illustrated in Figure 12-5 and Figure 12-6
  * and shows how PE1-4's routing tables can be controlled through route summarization.
trace: 12 Packet-switched underlay network – SRv6 based --> 12.3Scaling an SRv6 underlay infrastructure --> 12.3.1Route summarization and redistribution

It's also supported when redistributing routes between different routing domains, such as between Autonomous Systems using BGP-4.

text: To achieve more complex TE solutions, end-to-end visibility of the network is required, and a controller-based solution based on an SR-PCE is used. The SR-PCE receives detailed topology information via BGP-LS protocol from each domain. The SR-PCE then has a full picture of end to end reachability. When an ingress PE need to establish an end to end path it requests information from SR-PCE via PCEP protocol. SR-PCE responds with stack of SIDs to establish path to egress PE.

text: 13.1MP-BGP design
trace: 13Packet-switched Xhaul services Infrastructure --> 13.1MP-BGP design
