text:
* Both EVPN and MP-BGP L3VPNs use MP-BGP, with appropriate address-family support for
  * EVPN and L3VPN, to convey service connectivity information between Provider Edge \(PE\)
  * equipment.
  * Typically, the MP-BGP infrastructure for L2 and L3 services uses a Route Reflector design rather
  * than an I-BGP mesh between all PEs. In large networks, operators will normally implement a
  * hierarchical Route Reflector \(RR\) design for Multi-Protocol BGP \(MP–BGP\) peering. A pair of
  * Route Reflectors \(RR\) could be used at every domain to provide scalability and extensibility.

text: Latency sensitive and network control plane traffic should be forwarded using an expedited forwarding model as described in IETF RFC 3246\[66\]. In order to preserve minimum latency, these queues should be scheduled with a maximum of one packet in each queue and be allocated a priority forwarding schedule in the NPU. To prevent bandwidth starvation of non-priority scheduled traffic, each priority queue should be shaped or policed at a combined capacity less than the physical rate of each egress interface in the core, and with sufficient bandwidth capacity available

text:
* PE elements in the transport network domain will be responsible for providing logical separation
  * and encapsulation for transport. It can be assumed that there are two types of traffic that will be
  * presented for transport.
  * 1\. Ethernet frames. For example, RoE or eCPRI frames not using an IP header.
  * 2\. IP packets. For example, eCPRI packets or Backhaul traffic whose encapsulation includes an IP header.
  * 14.2.1Transport network domain PE ingress classification of Ethernet frames.
  * For the purposes of this section, it is assumed that there will be a physical or logical interface
  * attaching the Ethernet frame device to the transport network edge PE. As an example, this could be
  * a Mobile Client, such as a Front Haul Gateway or O-DU supporting an RU using RoE. PE nodes in
  * the transport network will perform classification on traffic ingressing the domain using different
  * models.

text:
* Admission control via policing should be applied to all sources of traffic at the PE. It is important to  
  * recognise that suitable capacity MUST be made available for all traffic \(especially where loss is
  * problematic\) in each element of the infrastructure. Where statistical multiplexing is expected to be
  * used to support additional service capacity in the network, excess traffic, beyond that which is
  * committed, MUST be marked as excess and be eligible for drop to protect other committed traffic
  * under heavy usage periods.
  * 14.2.4 PE Egress scheduling
  * Traffic arriving at a PE from the infrastructure, to be transmitted to a CE device should be done so
  * based on the model used for its classification on ingress.
  * 14.2.4.1 Unclassified traffic
  * Where an interface is using unclassified traffic, that is;
  * all traffic is always marked as default by the CE or
  * traffic with no marking available e.g. ethernet without a VLAN header,
  * traffic should be forwarded on a FIFO basis. In this model it must be ensured that the flow of traffic
  * into the PE toward the CE MUST be at a lower rate than the interface attaching the PE to the CE to
  * avoid congestion resulting in latency or loss.
  * 14.2.4.2 Classified traffic
  * Where an interface is using classified traffic, that is traffic has a marking scheme available, and
  * traffic is marked using this scheme, traffic should be forwarded to the CE with a queueing scheme
  * and scheduling model that is appropriate to the traffic for that CE. The specific marking and
  * queueing scheme are beyond the scope of this document but MUST be understood by the operator.
  * In this model the PE MUST support the classification and queueing of the CE destined traffic based
  * on the marking on the CE packet or frame. This is understood as "pipe model after" as defined in
  * IETF RFC 2983, section 5 6.

* Traffic from infrastructure to CE is transmitted based on classification model.
* Unclassified traffic (no marking) is forwarded FIFO with lower flow rates than interface attachment rate.
* Classified traffic (with marking scheme) uses queueing and scheduling models suitable for CE.

17Packet Switched TNE Security  
Packet Switched Transport Network Equipment \(TNE\) plays a vital role in building the transport  
infrastructure needed to support a 5G infrastructure. As such the packet switched TNEs needs to  
support a set of security features associated with:  
1\)  
The security of the TNEs \(both physical security nad user access security\)  
2\)  
The security of the network control, data and management plane protocols the TNEs run  
3\)  
Security functionality required by the TNEs to support security functionality required by the 5G  
mobile components.

RAN.WG11.Security-Requirements-Specifications  
\[27\]  
provides guidelines and requirements for  
security features required for an O-RAN compliant packet switched transport infrastructure.

physical security

unsecured, publicly accessible location.

rack with a partner or customer organization

text: To protect against DDoS attacks, typically filters and policers for host-bound exception traffic are used. The filters completely block specific types of control traffic \(for example, if OSPF is not used in particular deployment, there is no need to send OSPF packets to the TNE's control plane\), while policers specify rate limits for individual types of protocol control packets or for all control packet types for a protocol. Control traffic is dropped when it exceeds policer values. Each violation SHOULD immediately generates a notification to alert operators about a possible attack. The violation SHOULD be counted, the time that the violation starts noted, and the time of the last observed violation noted.

text: Network Slicing is end-to-end partitioning of the network resources and network functions so that selected applications/services/connections may run in isolation from each other for a specific business purpose. The overall slicing architecture is shown in Figure 18-1 and covers the orchestration infrastructure and at the physical layer can cover the radio access network, the mobile core, including data centers and virtualization aspects, and the X-haul transport network.

text:
* The packet-switched underlay network can use MPLS, SRv6 or a combination.
  * 18.1.1Underlay transport plane
  * The transport plane determines how traffic is sent over the packet-switched underlay infrastructure.
  * Four approaches are outlined for constructing the underlay transport plane/planes for a 5G transport
  * infrastructure. In each of the first three cases the level of resource sharing reduces, hence the slice
  * solution becomes harder in nature but may introduces scalability and operational challenges. Fourth
  * mapping approach is based on 5QI/DSCP, and scaling doesn't depend on the number of slices.
  * 18.1.2Single transport plane for all slices
  * The underlay network relies solely on the routing protocols \(IGPs and EGPs\) to calculate a single
  * forwarding table based on shortest path routing. The routing protocol sees all links and there is a
  * single forwarding table based on IGP and BGP metrics. All traffic takes the shortest path between
  * two points within the network and utilises ECMP.
  * In the context of slicing, all slices will see the same set of paths between end points within the
  * network. It can be considered the softest slicing solution in terms of the underlay transport plane.
  * However, although the infrastructure is shared between slices, it is highly scalable, widely
  * implemented in 4G and critical enterprise environments, and is capable of delivering high quality
  * SLAs.
  * 18.1.3Transport plane per 5G service type
  * Within the underlay network multiple transport planes are built to meet the specific forwarding
  * behaviors associated with the different 5G services types. One or more customers can then use these
  * transport planes. This is achieved using VPNs and traffic steering techniques. The transport planes
  * can utilise different topologies and be optimized based on different criteria. For example, a URLLC
  * service types could be optimised to use only the most reliable links in the network and select the
  * best paths between endpoints based on link delay metrics. In contrast, the eMBB service types
  * could be designed to use cheap, high bandwidth links, based on paths calculated with IGP metrics
  * correlated with link capacity \(high link capacity → low IGP metric\). And, NB-IoT service types,
  * which don't require neither low latency communication, nor high capacity, could use a 3rd transport
  * plane with paths established based on TE metrics, favoring links for this type of services. This
  * concept is outlined in Figure 18-4.

text: To implement such an approach, a mix of shortest path routing and traffic engineering solutions could be used. Traffic engineering options include flex-algo, SR-TE or traditional MPLS TE. As with any traffic engineering approach, consideration needs to be made of scale and state held within the network. Perhaps the simplest approach would be to use the default Flex-algorithm for eMBB and the mMTC services and a delay optimized flexible algorithm for the URLLC services. Backbone links and even nodes could be considered for inclusion or exclusion into the delay optimized flex-algorithm transport planes based on whether the algorithm is enabled on a TNE and TE affinities associated with the links.

text: The mapping between services and transport planes can be simplified with the usage of Color Extended Community defined in RFC 5512 \[100\]. Each transport plane \(each tunnel being part of specific transport plane\) is associated with some color value. For example, latency optimized tunnels use color 1 \(Transport Plane A\), capacity optimized tunnels use color 2 \(Transport Plane B\), and remaining tunnels use color 3 \(Transport Plane C\). At the same time, service prefixes are advertised via BGP with appropriate Color Extended Community. URLLC service prefixes use community value 1, eMBB service prefixes community value 2, and NB-IoT service prefixes community 3. On the PE router receiving such service prefixes, selection of appropriate transport plane is automatic based on matching colors advertised via Color Extended Community with the service prefix and the color associated with the transport plane.

text: 15 18.2.1Edge QoS
trace: 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network --> 9 18.2Quality of Service --> 15 18.2.1Edge QoS
text_preview: 15 18.2.1Edge QoS

text: Edge interfaces to packet transport networks are generally the slowest and also where congestion and packet drop most often occurs. Regardless of the QoS structures implemented in the transport core, it is important with slicing to support edge conditioning of traffic on ingress and scheduling on egress to the transport network. This ensures that each slice gets its contracted overall bandwidth and class bandwidth as it enters and leaves the transport network. When slices are presented via VLANs from the mobile clients, the PE router needs a hierarchical QoS capability that can account for the overall contracted bandwidth at the VLAN level and also the overall contracted class bandwidth within the VLAN.

text_preview: Edge interfaces to packet transport networks are often slow and prone to congestion. Implementing QoS structures with slicing ensures each slice gets its contracted bandwidth through edge conditioning on ingress and scheduling on egress. PE routers need hierarchical QoS capabilities that account for overall contracted bandwidth at the VLAN level.

text: 18.2.2.1 Shared queue architecture
trace: 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network --> 9 18.2Quality of Service --> 18.2.2.1 Shared queue architecture
text_preview: 18.2.2.1 Shared queue architecture

text: This approach follows the classic Diffserv QoS architecture. Slice traffic would be conditioned, and optionally marked or remarked as it enters the Diffserv domain, in this case the transport network. These markings determine the behaviour or Per Hop Behaviour \(PHB\) the traffic receives in the transport network. The number of PHBs in the core is determined by a number of factors; the number of PHBs that can be marked, the number of queues supported on the TNEs and operational complexity of the solution. Typically, in an MPLS network the traffic-class field is used to designate the PHB in the core. This is 3 bits, giving a maximum of 8 markings. In an IPv6 network the DSCP field is used to designate the PHB in the core. This is 6 bits giving a maximum of 64 markings. Even with more marking options, the number of PHBs in the core is generally kept small \(<8\) to simplify configuration, management and is generally done as a one-time set-up when a link is first installed. Core PHBs are enabled using a combination of queues, congestion management and scheduling techniques and are normally set-up in a work preserving fashion. That is, if one PHB is not fully utilised, the unused capacity can be used by traffic with other PHBs. Applying this to slicing. Each slice has an SLA based on overall and class bandwidth it receives. This is enforced on ingress at the PEs. In this QoS model, core queues are shared between slices and can be considered to be a soft form of slicing, but there is protection between slices through ingress edge conditioning of traffic. This architecture it is well tried, and tested, is simple and scales and able to support very tight SLAs.
trace: 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network --> 9 18.2Quality of Service --> 18.2.2.1 Shared queue architecture
text_preview: This approach follows the classic Diffserv QoS architecture. Slice traffic is conditioned and marked as it enters the transport network, determining Per Hop Behaviour (PHB). PHBs depend on marking options, queue support, and complexity. In MPLS networks, up to 8 PHBs are enabled using queues, congestion management, and scheduling techniques.

text: 18.2.2.2 Dedicated queue architecture
trace: 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network --> 9 18.2Quality of Service --> 18.2.2.2 Dedicated queue architecture
text_preview: 18.2.2.2 Dedicated queue architecture

text: This approach uses the same Diffserv QoS architecture, except one or more PHBs is exclusively dedicated to a particular slice or slice type. An example could be a high priority PHB, which is dedicated exclusively to the URLLC slice. At the same time other slices can share the remaining PHBs. Given the small numbers of queues normally provisioned in the core \(and available traffic classes in an MPLS environment\), this type of solution needs to be used with extreme care, however it is a model used today successfully in production networks to support private line services which run in a dedicated high priority queue, while simultaneously supporting other services using a shared queue architecture.
trace: 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network --> 9 18.2Quality of Service --> 18.2.2.2 Dedicated queue architecture
text_preview: This approach uses Diffserv QoS architecture, but one or more PHBs are exclusively dedicated to a particular slice or type, such as URLLC. Other slices share remaining PHBs, requiring care due to limited queues in core networks.

text: 18.2.2.3 Dedicated links and queues per slice
trace: 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network --> 9 18.2Quality of Service --> 18.2.2.3 Dedicated links and queues per slice
text_preview: 18.2.2.3 Dedicated links and queues per slice

text: This QoS approach achieves hard slicing by either dedicating core links or parts of a core link to a specific slice. This can be achieved by one of the following approaches:
trace: 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network --> 9 18.2Quality of Service --> 18.2.2.3 Dedicated links and queues per slice
text_preview: This QoS approach achieves hard slicing by either dedicating core links or parts of a core link to a specific slice. This can be achieved by one of the following approaches:

text:
* Using dedicated links per slice in the transport network. This could be done using full physical Ethernet interfaces or using Ethernet TDM technology, such as flexE, to create dedicated Ethernet channels for different slices. Within these links, class-based queuing would be used to support different traffic types associated with the slice. This approach offers no ability to share unused bandwidth between slices as the links are hard partitioned.
  * Using hierarchically scheduled bandwidth on core links. In this case core links would be split using a shaper to govern the level of bandwidth available to each slice, with class-based queuing within the shaped bandwidth. This approach does offer the ability to share unused bandwidth between slices.
trace: 18 5G Slicing in a packet switched Xhaul network --> 9 18.2Quality of Service --> 18.2.2.3 Dedicated links and queues per slice
text_preview:
* Using dedicated links per slice: full Ethernet interfaces or flexE technology create separate channels for each slice. Class-based queuing supports different traffic types.
* Hierarchically scheduled bandwidth on core links: shapers govern bandwidth levels, with class-based queuing within shaped bandwidth. This approach shares unused bandwidth between slices.

text: In addition to dividing the core bandwidth up, mechanisms are required to guide slice traffic into the links or shaped bandwidth associated with each slice. Slice traffic could be guided into the appropriate links using a TE solution, such as flex-algo or SR-TE or alternatively the core routers

text: Here the purpose is to improve the energy consumption of a network by implementing mechanisms that can dynamically optimize such consumption according to network status and conditions. Some events need to be identified as triggers for such optimization, that could require of smart management and control capabilities to make the network adapt to the observed circumstances, while reducing energy. Actions that could lay on this set are for instance:

text_preview:

- Smart management
- Energy reduction 
- Adaptation to circumstances

text:
* Concentration of traffic flows in some links during low-activity periods, then freeing up some of the links for reducing the consumption on the corresponding TNEs. This could be done by the transport network in an isolated manner, or as part of a combined radio- transport optimization scenario. Note that additional capabilities are needed at device level for taking advantage of the links becoming empty as consequence of the traffic consolidation.
  * Exposure of energy per path or topology based on the consumption of the participating individual devices, so that upper management systems can build an overall view of the energy consumption map for taking decisions \(e.g., function placement, traffic consolidation as before, etc\).

text: Fixed systems \(Figure 19-1\) are typically 1 RU or 2 RU devices, which do not have replacable network modules. Modular chassis \(Figure 19-2\), on the other hand, are typically bigger devices, with flexible hardware options \(line cards, modules\). text:
* 6 Pluggable optical modules inserted into the system. Responsible for electric optic 7 conversion of the signal. Energy consumption of pluggable optical modules can greatly 8 vary, depending on the module type. For example, 800 Gbps optical module consumes 9 significantly more energy than 1 Gbps optical module. Similarly, long range or extended 10 range optical module consumes significantly more energy than short range optical module. 11 Additionally, energy consumption might depend on the traffic load. Some optical modules, 12 the so called Power over Ethernet \(PoE\) optical modules, can also provide power to the 13 attached end-user equipment \(e.g. small in-house O-RU\), which considerably increases the 14 energy drawn by the optical module.
  * 15 Physical Layer \(PHY\). Dedicated chipset responsible for providing an electrical, 16 mechanical, and procedural interface to the transmission medium. Energy consumption 17 might depend on the features supported by PHY.
  * 18 Packet Forwarding Engine \(PFE\). Called as well Network Processing Unit \(NPU\). It is a 19 dedicated chipset \(or group of chipsets\) responsible for TN data plane, switching frames or 20 routing packets from one port to another port of the device. PFE/NPU energy consumption 21 increases with increased traffic volume \(for example, 800 Gbps PFE/NPU, consumes 22 significantly more energy than 1 Gbps PFE/NPU\), as well as with features supported and 23 enabled on the port \(for example, enabling MACsec or IPsec encryption might increase the 24 energy consumption\).
  * 25 Central Processing Unit \(CPU\) and Double Data Rate Synchronous Dynamic Random-26 Access Memory \(DDR-RAM\). In TNEs, CPUs together DDR-RAM, are responsible for 27 handling transport network control plane, processing messages exchanged by various 28 transport network protocols \(IGP, BGP, LDP, …\). Control plane load, for example sizes of 29 the routing and forwarding tables that must be maintained, number of IGP/BGP peers, 30 inbound/outbound route policy complexity, etc. have effect on energy consumption. 31 Additionally, modular chassis design relies on distributed control plane, with additional 32 CPUs and DDR-RAMs in the line cards \(LCs\).

Some additional functions \(for example, PTP handling, IPsec or MACsec encryption\) might be implemented via dedicated Application-Specific Integrated Circuits \(ASICs\) or Field Programmable Gateway Arrays \(FPGAs\). These circuits consume energy to fulfill their functions.
  * Fans. Fans are used to improve heat dissipation from the device. Fans energy consumption increases with the temperature. text: • Flexible, fully programmable versus fixed pipeline PFE chipsets
trace: 19 Energy efficiency in the context of Xhaul Packet Switched Transport Network Equipments --> 19.3.4PFE energy optimization
text_preview: • Flexible, fully programmable versus fixed pipeline PFE chipsets

text: PFE chipsets can be divided into two main categories: flexible, fully programmable \(1\), and fixed pipeline, with limited programmability \(2\). Fixed pipeline chipsets consume less energy \(Figure 19-7\), as their design is simpler – they are designed to perform predetermined functions \(for example, to do the MPLS switching\) with limited flexibility to program other functions \(for example, perform SRv6 encapsulation/decapsulation, if the chipset was not designed from day one to perform this function\). Therefore, to support particular throughput, they require less transistors comparing to flexible, fully programmable chipsets. This results in lower energy consumption. However, the tradeoff is feature flexibility offered by flexible, fully programmable PFE chipsets.

This results in lower energy consumption compared to flexible, fully programmable chipsets, but at the cost of reduced feature flexibility.

text: 19.3.6 Switching fabric energy optimization
trace: 19 Energy efficiency in the context of Xhaul Packet Switched Transport Network Equipments --> 19.3.4PFE energy optimization --> 19.3.6 Switching fabric energy optimization
text_preview: 19.3.6 Switching fabric energy optimization

text: Switching fabric complex contains fabric ASICs, and SerDes complexes interconnecting fabric ASICs with PFEs \(Figure 19-2\). Therefore, in fabric complex, energy could be saved by switching off fabric ASICs or fabric SerDes complexes.
trace: 19 Energy efficiency in the context of Xhaul Packet Switched Transport Network Equipments --> 19.3.4PFE energy optimization --> 19.3.6 Switching fabric energy optimization
text_preview: Switching fabric complex contains fabric ASICs, and SerDes complexes interconnecting fabric ASICs with PFEs \(Figure 19-2\). Therefore, in fabric complex, energy could be saved by switching off fabric ASICs or fabric SerDes complexes.

text: There are couple of possible options for switch fabric design, when it comes to fabric redundancy in modular chassis. One of the common switching fabric redundancy designs is N+1 redundancy, where 'N' fabric interface boards provide capacity sufficient to interconnect all PFEs, and there is +1 fabric interface board as spare. For example, if the node has 8 PFEs, each PFE with 500 Gbps, the required switching fabric capacity is 4 Tbps. If the capacity of single fabric ASICs is 500 Gbps, and single fabric interface board hosts two fabric ASIC \(1 Tbps per FIB\), equipping the node with 5 fabric interface boards \(5 Tbps in total\) would provide N+1 switching fabric redundancy.
trace: 19 Energy efficiency in the context of Xhaul Packet Switched Transport Network Equipments --> 19.3.4PFE energy optimization --> 19.3.6 Switching fabric energy optimization
text_preview: There are couple of options for switch fabric design, particularly N+1 redundancy. This design provides sufficient capacity to interconnect all PFEs with a spare board. For example, if a node has 8 PFEs (500 Gbps each), it requires 4 Tbps switching fabric capacity.

text: In case of single fabric interface board failure, the switching fabric is still able to provide full required capacity of 4 Tbps. However, when two fabric interface boards fail, the maximum fabric capacity is reduced to 3 Tbps only. In order to provide protection for two fabric interface boards failures, N+2 \(two "spare" fabric interface boards\) redundancy mode would be required.
trace: 19 Energy efficiency in the context of Xhaul Packet Switched Transport Network Equipments --> 19.3.4PFE energy optimization --> 19.3.6 Switching fabric energy optimization
text_preview: In case of single fabric interface board failure, the switching fabric provides full capacity (4 Tbps). However, with two failed boards, capacity drops to 3 Tbps. To protect against this, an N+2 redundancy mode is needed for two spare fabric interface boards.

text: The logical underlay is illustrated in Figure 20-3 and consists of QoS enabled infrastructure that either uses an IP/MPLS or an SRv6 underlay data and control plane. It provides any-to-any connectivity between TNEs in the network, regardless of whether they reside in the same metro network, a different metro network or the transport core and supports both shortest path routing and traffic engineering. The underlay data planes, control plane and scaling mechanisms to enable this for IP/MPLS and SRv6 are different and discussed in their respective chapters. Both solutions have the capabilities to support best effort and traffic engineered forwarding and the capability to create discrete constrained based topologies using either traditional traffic engineering or flexible algorithm which can be optimized on criteria such as shortest path, delay and bandwidth.

text: 20.2.1Underlay Quality of Service \(QoS\)
trace: 20 Supporting mobile scenarios on a packet switched Xhaul network --> 20.2.1Underlay Quality of Service \(QoS\)
text_preview: 20.2.1Underlay Quality of Service \(QoS\)

text: Refer to section 14 for fuller discussion on QoS. Underlay QoS refers to the scheduling used on the core or backbone links. All backbone links are enabled with a combination of priority and class- based queueing. Assignment of traffic to different queues within the core is based on marking within the packet header. In an MPLS backbone this is based on the EXP bits or traffic class field, a three-bit field, giving a maximum number of core behaviours of eight. In an IPv6 backbone this is based on the DSCP bits, a six-bit field, giving a maximum number of 64 markings and potential behaviours.

text:
* For mobile services it is proposed to use BGP based VPNs to overlay service functionality onto the underlay transport network as described in section 13.

text: 20.4.1.1 Assumptions
trace: 20 Supporting mobile scenarios on a packet switched Xhaul network --> 20.4Mobile services --> 20.4.1.1 Assumptions
text_preview: 20.4.1.1 Assumptions

text:
* 1\. 7.2x C/U planes connects to the transport network via a VLAN on a physical Ethernet interfaces on O-RUs and O-DUs.
  * 2\. 7.2x C/U planes traffic uses Ethernet / VLAN encapsulation option and not the optional Ethernet / VLAN / IP encapsulation.
  * 3\. 7.2x C/U planes uses an Ethernet service across the transport network to connect O-RUs to O-DUs. This is via an Ethernet VPWS service using EVPN in the transport network.
  * 4\. If the 7.2x C/U planes traffic used an Ethernet / VLAN / IP encapsulation, then the transport network could use a L3 VPN service to transport the traffic between the O-RU and the O-DU, but this is not considered in the following sections.
  * 5\. 7.2x M-plane connects to the transport network via a VLAN on a physical Ethernet.
  * 6\. 7.2x M-plane uses an Ethernet / VLAN / IP encapsulation.
  * 7\. 7.2x M-plane is operating in hybrid mode and uses an L3 VPN service across the transport network to connect O-RUs, O-DUs and O-RAN NMS together. This is via an overlay MP-BGP based L3VPN.
  * 8\. For the following discussion, the 7.2x C/U planes and M plane share a single physical Ethernet interface on the O-RU towards the CSR with the C/U plane and M-Plane running in different VLANs.
  * 9\. Each O-RU has its own dedicated Ethernet port on the CSR. I.E There is no lower level aggregation of statistical multiplexing component between an O-RU and the CSR.
  * 10\. O-RU and O-DU set appropriate QoS markings for C/U and M-plane traffic that the transport network can trust. In other words, the TNE does not need to classify different components of Fronthaul for transport.
  * 20.4.1.2 Open Fronthaul physical design
  * 1\. 3 O-RUs per cell site.
  * 2\. In the above example, each O-RU is connected via a dedicated Ethernet interface to a co- located CSR. This single Ethernet supports both the C/U planes and the M-plane presented through two VLANs. The required capacity of the Ethernet link between the O-RU and the CSR is primarily dependent on the O-RU's radio capabilities. The requirements document \[20\] provides some bandwidth examples for Open Fronthaul bandwidth. The expectation is that the C/U plane traffic will be significantly larger than the M-Plane traffic, therefore these Ethernet interfaces should be provisioned to deal with the peak 7.2x C/U-plane traffic of an O-RU. It should be noted that unlike CPRI, the 7.2x C/U plane traffic loads are dependent on user activity, so peak loading will only occur when the O-RU is running at full theoretical capacity.

text: 3\. In the above example, each CSR is connected using a single Ethernet link across dark fibre to the HSR. Other underlay transport technologies and topologies are available, such as redundant hub and spoke, chain or ring topologies in the access network. Regardless of the WAN technology and topology employed, careful consideration needs to be given the latency and jitter requirements of C/U plane traffic between the O-RU and the O-DU. Transport considerations includes fibre distances between the O-RU and the O-DU, the number of routers/switches traversed, link speeds and switching times of the intermediate transport network equipment. \(see section 10.1.1.2 for more details\). As O-RAN 7.2x traffic loads are dependent on user activity and in the example there are multiple O-RUs in the cell site, the link capacity between the CSR and HSR does not need to be provisioned at the theoretical sum of the O-RU's peak rates because a statistical gain can be realised. The bandwidth provisioning should be based on usage and the real achievable peak rates associated with the O-RUs. The real achievable peak rates are dependent on factors such as number and proximity of radios to each other and environmental factors. Precise provisioning rules for 5G Fronthaul is subject to further investigation.

text:
* 1\. The QoS scheme outlined in section 20.2.1, Figure 20-4 will be applied across the transport network and is capable of supporting Fronthaul, Midhaul and Backhaul traffic running on the same link. If an SRv6 underlay is to be used, then at a minimum the same queue structure supported by appropriate operator selected DSCP marking should be used.
  * 2\. O-RU and O-DU set appropriate QoS markings for C/U and M-plane traffic that transport network can trust.
  * 3\. In the above example, the C/U and M-plane traffic share the same physical interface, separated using VLANs between the O-RU and CSR and between HSR and O-DU. In this situation the mobile components \(O-RUs and O-DUs\) will need to support:
  * o An internal scheduling mechanism to prioritise C/U plane traffic over M-Plane traffic onto the Ethernet interface
  * o Depending on O-RU→ CSR and HSR→ O-DU link speeds, the O-RU, O-DU, CSR and HSR may need to support TSN frame pre-emption to control serialization delay. \(refer to section 10.1.1.2.1 for more details\). Alternatively, if the O-RU or CSR do not support TSN frame pre-emption or the O-DU or HSR do not support TSN frame pre-emption, then separate physical interfaces could be used to separate the C/U plane and M-plane traffic.
  * 5\. C/U and M-plane traffic from all O-RUs in the cell site share the same transport link between the CSR and the HSR. In most scenarios where a CSR supports multiple radios running fronthaul, this link will be 25Gbps or above and therefore does not really benefit from TSN frame pre-emption. However, in some instances, the link between the CSR and HSR may be lower speed and would benefit from TSN frame pre-emption. \(see section 10.1.1.2.1 for more details\)
  * 6\. C/U plane traffic must be prioritized over M-plane traffic on the WAN links. CSR and HSR must be provisioned at both the link level and within the link level queuing infrastructure in a manner such that C/U plane traffic is not dropped or experiences queuing delay in either the CSR or HSR \(or any additional Transport Network Equipment in the path between the O-RU and the O-DU\). M-plane traffic can experience a level of delay, so be configured to use a lower priority queue or a queuing scheme such as Weighted Round Robin that reserves a small amount of bandwidth for management traffic \(see section 14 for an example\)

text:
* 1\. C/U plane traffic uses an EVPN VPWS service to transport traffic between the O-RU and O- DU over the access network. To simplify cell site VLAN provisioning, common VLANs could be used between the O-RUs and the CSR and VLAN tag translation could occur on the HSR to provide a unique interface / VLAN id per O-RU towards the O-DU. Depending on the capabilities of the O-DU, EVPN has mechanisms that can provide service level resiliency but this is dependent on the O-DU network implementation.
  * 2\. The M-plane traffic on the O-RU and O-DU connects, via a VLAN or physical interface to a MP-BGP based L3 VPN service. This provides layer 3 connectivity between the management components on the O-RU, O-DU and the O-RAN "Network Management System" \(NMS\). "Route Target" filtering could be used to restrict transport level connectivity between management entities. For example, the transport network could be configured such that IP connectivity is only permitted between the NMS and the O-DUs and O-RUs, while no IP connectivity is permitted between O-RUs.

text: The following design assumptions have been made about the Midhaul / Backhaul components and how traffic is presented and moved across the transport network.

text_preview: The following design assumptions have been made about the Midhaul / Backhaul components and how traffic is presented and moved across the transport network.

text: 20.4.3.1 Assumptions
trace: 20 Supporting mobile scenarios on a packet switched Xhaul network --> 20.4.2Non O-RAN Fronthaul --> 20.4.3.1 Assumptions
text_preview: 20.4.3.1 Assumptions

text:
* 1\. Midhaul and Backhaul traffic share the same L3 VPNs.
  * 2\. There are dedicated and separate L3 VPNs for control plane traffic \(N1, N2\) and user plane traffic \(N3 and N9\).
  * 3\. If legacy Backhaul is required, it shares the same L3 VPN transport services used by the 5G EMBB Midhaul and Backhaul user and control plane infrastructure.
  * 4\. If there are multiple Midhaul and Backhaul transport slices, they could run in their own independent L3 VPNs \(see Annex F: Transport network slicing solution for WG1 Slicing \(informational\)\)
  * 5\. Midhaul and Backhaul mobile components will either use a discrete independent VLAN or a dedicated physical Ethernet to separate control and user plane traffic. For the following discussion it is assumed they are presented via VLANs on a single Ethernet interface.
  * 6\. Midhaul and Backhaul mobile components which require connectivity to different transport slices will either use a discrete VLAN or a dedicated physical interfaces per slice. For the following discussion it is assumed they will be presented via VLANs.
  * 7\. The transport and RAN teams have collaborated on Midhaul / Backhaul QoS marking and packets emerging from O-DUs, O-CUs and UPFs have a DSCP marking appropriate to their 5G forwarding requirements, and the TNEs can trust these markings.
  * 8\. N6 networks associated with different customers, applications or use cases will use L3 VPNs.

text: Note: Other service designs could be considered, for example a design where only Ethernet services are used from the cell site and the hub sites and L3 VPN services are built at the hub sites. The primary reason for the choice outlined above is to make the service orchestration as simple as possible, so services only need to be configured where the mobile clients connect to the transport network and no intermediate stitching points within the transport network are needed.
trace: 20 Supporting mobile scenarios on a packet switched Xhaul network --> 20.4.2Non O-RAN Fronthaul --> 20.4.3.1 Assumptions
text_preview:
To simplify service orchestration, we choose a design where:

* Only Ethernet services are used from cell sites
* L3 VPN services are built at hub sites
* This reduces the need for intermediate stitching points in the transport network, making it simpler to configure services only where mobile clients connect to the transport network.

text: 20.4.3.2 Midhaul and Backhaul physical topology
trace: 20 Supporting mobile scenarios on a packet switched Xhaul network --> 20.4.2Non O-RAN Fronthaul --> 20.4.3.2 Midhaul and Backhaul physical topology
text_preview: 20.4.3.2 Midhaul and Backhaul physical topology

text:
* 1\. O-DUs connect, via Ethernet interface/interfaces, to a co-located HSR or CSR. The Ethernet interface/interfaces support Midhaul control and user plane traffic via two discrete VLANs.
  * 2\. O-CUs connect, via Ethernet interfaces to the transport network. The O-CU Ethernet interface/interfaces support Midhaul and Backhaul control and user plane traffic via two discrete VLANs.
  * 3\. The UPFs connect, via Ethernet interfaces to the transport network. The UPF connects to the common control and user plane Midhaul/Backhaul VPNs.
  * 4\. The location of the O-CUs and UPFs is service dependent and the choice of the operator. Additionally, these components may be virtualized or containerized and reside in a data center. In these scenarios, orchestration techniques maybe be required to connect the virtualized O-DU, O-CU and UPF components in the data centers to the correct WAN L3VPNs.
  * 5\. 5G Core components connect via Ethernet interfaces to the transport network in their respective locations. These components may be virtualized or containerized and reside in a data center. In these scenarios, orchestration techniques are required to connect the 5G control plane entities in the data centers to the Midhaul and Backhaul control plane WAN L3VPNs.

text:
* 6\. O-CU can reside in the same location as the O-DUs it controls, therefore Midhaul traffic never leaves the site and is switched between the two entities by the either the CSR or HSR. Alternatively, the O-CU can reside in a different location to the O-DUs it controls. In this case the Midhaul traffic traverses the WAN.
  * 7\. HSRs provides the boundary between the access and aggregation networks. Connectivity to the aggregation network will typically use high-capacity Ethernet interfaces or bundles of high capacity Ethernet interface. The topology of the aggregation network is normally resilient, but topologies vary based on operator choices and constraints, with hub and spoke and rings very common.
  * 8\. Midhaul and Backhaul user plane traffic levels are dependent on UE usage, the characteristics of the radio and the number the proximity of radios to each other. The O-RAN Transport Requirements document \[20\] outlines some of the provisioning rules widely used in planning 4G Backhaul networks. Although not directly applicable to the 5G, they provide a good starting point in terms. Longer term network capacity planning should be done based on monitoring and modelling the live network.

text_preview:
* 6\. O-CU can coexist with controlled O-DUs, with Midhaul traffic switched by CSR or HSR.
* 7\. HSR defines network boundaries using high-capacity Ethernet interfaces.
* 8\. Midhaul and Backhaul traffic levels depend on UE usage, radio characteristics, and proximity.

trace: 20 Supporting mobile scenarios on a packet switched Xhaul network --> 20.4.2Non O-RAN Fronthaul --> 20.4.3.3 QoS

text:
* 1\. O-CU and UPFs mark the packets they produce based on the behaviour required for the mobile data the carry.
  * 2\. Most Midhaul and Backhaul traffic is far more tolerant to delay, and jitter compared with Fronthaul traffic. The exception could be some URLLC based use-cases. However, for most 5G use-cases fibre propagation delay, number of hops, transport equipment switching times and serialization delays are not of a huge issue when designing Midhaul and Backhaul networks.
  * 3\. In some scenarios, particularly when some forms of slicing are considered then edge QoS in the form of ingress and egress H-QoS will be required.
trace: 20 Supporting mobile scenarios on a packet switched Xhaul network --> 20.4.2Non O-RAN Fronthaul --> 20.4.3.3 QoS
text_preview:
O-CU and UPFs mark packets based on mobile data behavior.
Midhaul and Backhaul traffic tolerate delay and jitter, except for URLLC use-cases.
Fibre propagation delays are not a major issue in Midhaul and Backhaul networks.
Edge QoS may be required for some forms of slicing.

text: Background
trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Background
text_preview: Background

text: The Internet and role of packet switching has changed over the last couple of decades and continues to evolve rapidly. This is no better illustrated than by the 5G transport requirements which anticipates billions of endpoints, massive numbers of antenna, huge bandwidths and the ability to concurrently support different 5G services. This evolution is challenging existing Internet protocols, equipment and increasing the operational complexity of the network. Segment Routing and related technology evolutions aims to address these challenges through protocol simplification, removal of state from the network and embracing technology advances such as Software Defined Networking.
trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Background
text_preview: The Internet has undergone significant changes over the last couple of decades, driven by packet switching. 5G transport requirements illustrate this evolution with billions of endpoints, massive antennas, huge bandwidths, and concurrent support for multiple services. Segment Routing addresses these challenges through protocol simplification and Software Defined Networking advancements.

text: Segment Routing
trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Segment Routing
text_preview: Segment Routing

text: Segment Routing \(SR\) is based on the loose Source Routing concept. A node can include an ordered list of instructions in the packet headers. These instructions steer the forwarding and the processing of the packet along its path in the network. Single instructions are called segments, a sequence of instructions is called a segment list or an SR Policy. Each segment can enforce a topological requirement \(e.g. pass through a node or an interface\) or a service requirement \(e.g. execute an operation on the packet\). The term segment refers to the fact that a network path towards a destination can be split in segments by adding intermediate waypoints. The segment list can be included by the original source of the packet or by an intermediate node. When the segment list is inserted by an intermediate node, it can be removed by another node along the path of the packet, supporting the concept of tunneling through an SR domain from an ingress node to an egress node. The implementation of the Segment Routing Architecture requires a data plane which is able to carry the segment lists in the packet headers and to properly process them. Control plane operations complement the data plane functionality, allowing segment allocation \(i.e. associate a segment identifier to a specific instruction in a node\) and distribution of segment identifiers within an SR domain.
trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Segment Routing
text_preview: Segment Routing (SR) uses loose Source Routing with ordered lists of instructions in packet headers. These instructions steer forwarding and processing along the network path, enforcing topological requirements at each segment. Segment lists can be inserted by source or intermediate nodes, allowing tunneling through SR domains from ingress to egress nodes.

text: Segment Routing architectural principle
trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Segment Routing --> Segment Routing architectural principle
text_preview: Segment Routing architectural principle

text: There is a single SR architecture which is defined in RFC8402 \[139\]. This defines the general concepts of SR and is independent from the specific data plane. Currently, there are two instantiations of the SR architecture designed and implemented in production code, SR over MPLS \(SR-MPLS\) and SR over IPv6 \(SRv6\).
trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Segment Routing --> Segment Routing architectural principle
text_preview: There is a single SR architecture defined in RFC8402 [139]. It defines general concepts independent of the data plane. Two instantiations are SR over MPLS (SR-MPLS) and SR over IPv6 (SRv6).

trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Segment Routing --> Segment Routing architectural principle

text: The architecture relies on segments identifiers \(SIDs\) and SID lists. The SID represents a single instruction which can be related to how the packet is forwarded or a function that needs to be performed on a packet. A SID lists or the SR policy is a collection of SIDs or instructions to be performed on the packet as it traverses the SR domain. Typically, a SID list is imposed on the packets as it enters the SR domain and is either empty or completed by the time it leaves an SR domain.
trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Segment Routing --> Segment Routing architectural principle
text_preview: The architecture relies on segments identifiers (SIDs) and SID lists. A SID represents a single instruction for packet forwarding or function. A SID list, or SR policy, is a collection of SIDs to be performed as packets traverse the SR domain. Typically, a SID list is imposed at entry and completed by exit.

text: There are two basic types of segment, global segments which correspond to instructions that are globally valid in an SR domain and local segments which correspond to instructions that are only valid within a single node. Some of the key segment types are:
trace: 21 Annex A: Overview of "Segment Routing" \(SR\) --> Segment Routing --> Segment Routing architectural principle
text_preview: There are two basic types of segment, global segments which correspond to instructions that are globally valid in an SR domain and local segments which correspond to instructions that are only valid within a single node. Some of the key segment types are:

text:
* 1\. IGP Prefix and IGP node segments: These are global SIDs and are instructions on how to forward a packet towards a destination IP network or destination IP node. As the name suggests these are conveyed by IGP and can be used by any node in the SR domain to send traffic to a node or IP prefix.
  * 2\. Adjacency segments: These are local SIDs which identify the links available on that node.
  * 3\. Anycast segments: These are a special IGP-prefix segment that corresponds to an anycast prefix. ie a prefix advertised by more than one router. Anycast and anycast segments are commonly used to provide high availability or load balancing solutions.
  * 4\. Binding Segments: These are a single SID that is associated with a segment list or SR policy. This means the node that processes the Binding SID replaces the single segment with a segment list.

IGP Prefix and Node Segments: Global SIDs for forwarding packets to destination IP networks or nodes.
Adjacency Segments: Local SIDs identifying links on a node.
Anycast Segments: Special IGP-prefix segments for high availability or load balancing.
Binding Segments: Single SIDs associated with segment lists or SR policies.

text:
* 1\. A dynamically locally computed forwarding path between an ingress and egress point within the SR domain by the ingress node either imposing the node SID of the egress node or the prefix SID of the destination prefix. Typically, a link-state IGP or an EGP routing protocol, running locally on the routers calculate these types of paths and they exhibit the behaviour of normal routing protocols such "Shortest Path Forwarding" and "Equal Cost Multi Pathing \(ECMP\)
  * 2\. A fully deterministic path between the ingress and egress points. In this case the SR policy or SID list includes all nodes on the path and if required adjacency SIDs to select links between nodes.
  * 3\. A combination of the two. The SR architecture can build a path between an ingress and egress node that combines dynamically computed forwarding and explicitly routed forwarding.

text:
* Two data plane instantiations are designed and implement: SR over MPLS \(SR-MPLS\) and SR over
  * IPv6 \(SRv6\).
  * SR-MPLS
  * The MPLS data plane \(SR-MPLS\) is specified in RFC 8660 "Segment Routing with MPLS data
  * plane"\[146\], In the case of SR-MPLS, Segment Routing does not require any change to the MPLS
  * forwarding plane. An SR Policy is instantiated through the MPLS Label Stack and the Segment IDs
  * \(SIDs\) of a Segment List are inserted as MPLS Labels. The classical forwarding functions available
  * for MPLS networks allow implementing the SR operations.
  * IPv6 data plane \(SRv6\)
  * For the IPv6 data plane \(SRv6\), a new type of IPv6 Routing Extension Header, called Segment
  * Routing Header \(SRH\) has been defined in RFC 8754 IPv6 Segment Routing Header \(SRH\) \[151\].
  * The SRH contains the Segment List \(SR Policy\) as an ordered list of IPv6 addresses: each address
  * in the list is a SID. A dedicated field, referred to as Segments Left, is used to maintain the pointer to
  * the active SID of the Segment List. This SRH format and basic operation of the SRH is illustrated
  * in Figure 21-2.

text: In addition to the basic operations, the SRv6 Network Programming model \[154\] describes a set of functions that can be associated to segments and executed in a given SRv6 node. Examples of such functions are: different types of packet encapsulation \(e.g. IPv6 in IPv6, IPv4 in IPv6, Ethernet in IPv6\), corresponding decapsulation, lookup operation on a specific routing table \(e.g. to support VPNs\). The list of functions described in \[154\] is not meant to be exhaustive, as any function can be associated to a segment identifier in a node. Obviously, the definition of a standardized set of segment routing functions facilitates the deployment of SR domains with interoperable equipment from multiple vendors.

text: The hybrid control plane is combination of distributed control plane and centralised SDN control plane functionality. Like the central control plane model there is no universal architecture for a hybrid control plane design, other than some functions are provided centrally and others occur locally on the TNEs. One of the most common hybrid control plane designs is where the central SDN controllers provides a "Path Computation Element" capability. In this model the PCE is responsible for path computation and inter-domain routing with the distributed control planes running on the TNEs, responsible for building the link state database, calculating the network graph and building the shortest path forwarding tables. In this scenario there is generally a tight relationship between the two components.

text: EVPN E-Line service
trace: 22 Annex B: IETF Ethernet Virtual Private Networks --> EVPN E-Line service
text_preview: EVPN E-Line service

text: EVN E-Line, called as well EVPN Virtual Private Wire Service \(VPWS\), is point-to-point Layer 2 service, without MAC learning. Ethernet frame received from an end device connected via single-homed or multi-homed attachment circuit, is transported over this point-to-point service to the remote end device, connected again via single-homed or multi-homed attachment circuit. Since it is pure point-to-point communication, no MAC learning is required, and thus MAC learning is not part of EVPN E-Line \(VPWS\) architecture.

text_preview: EVPN Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) is a Layer 2, point-to-point service without MAC learning. Ethernet frames from end devices are transported to remote ends via the same type of circuit, eliminating the need for MAC learning due to pure point-to-point communication.

trace: 22 Annex B: IETF Ethernet Virtual Private Networks --> EVPN VLAN-bundle service

text: The biggest challenge with basic EVPN VLAN-based service is scaling. In EVPN VLAN-based service each VLAN consumes dedicated EVI, thus the maximum numbers of VLANs that can be served is limited by the supported EVIs on given hardware platform. EVPN VLAN-bundle service addresses this scaling limitation by bundling multiple VLANs into single bridge \(MAC learning\) domain/table and single EVI \(MAC-VRF\), as outlined in Figure 22-5

text: The first restriction is related to the fact, that underlying transport identification \(i.e. MPLS label with MPLS underlay transport, Function:Argument with SRv6 underlay transport\) identifies the bridge domain. Therefore, the underlying transport identification cannot be used to distinguish Ethernet frames - received over EVPN network - as belonging to different VLANs, if VLAN tag is stripped before sending Ethernet frames across EVPN. And this differentiation is required to maintain per-VLAN broadcast/flooding restrictions.

This is crucial for maintaining per-VLAN broadcast/flooding restrictions.

trace: 18 23 Annex C: MP-BGP based L3VPNs
text_preview: 18 23 Annex C: MP-BGP based L3VPNs

text: BGP based layer 3 VPNs are a widely deployed connectivity application in Service Provider networks and work over an MPLS and SRv6 underlay infrastructure. BGP based layer 3 VPNs are based on RFC4364 \[88\] and use a peer-to-peer model that uses Border Gateway Protocol \(BGP\) to distribute VPN-related information. It is a highly scalable, peer-to-peer model that through route filtering allows flexible connectivity models within a VPN. VPN topologies include any-to-any L3 multi-point solutions as well as L3 tree solutions where connectivity constraints are built into the VPN infrastructure through controlled exportations and importation of routing information. This makes it an effective and efficient technology for L3 services associated with Xhaul transport.

They use a peer-to-peer model that distributes VPN-related info using BGP (RFC4364), enabling flexible connectivity through route filtering and controlled routing information exchange.

text: Route Targets \(RT\) are the mechanism by routing information distribution can be controlled within an BGP based VPN throughout the packet switched network. Route Target are propagated through the BGP based VPN network using route-target extended MP-BGP communities. text: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service
text_preview: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service

text: This annex gives an overview of packet base Quality of Service \(QoS\).
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service
text_preview: This annex gives an overview of packet base Quality of Service \(QoS\).

text: What is Quality of Service?
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> What is Quality of Service?
text_preview: What is Quality of Service?

text: Quality of Service \(QoS\) is an umbrella term that broadly covers the concept of the management of traffic flowing in an infrastructure. In general, QoS can provide two capabilities.
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> What is Quality of Service?
text_preview: Quality of Service \(QoS\) is an umbrella term that broadly covers the concept of the management of traffic flowing in an infrastructure. In general, QoS can provide two capabilities.

trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> What is Quality of Service?

text:
* 1\. A mechanism to actively manage the transmission of data on a network link out of a node when the link is approaching or at saturation. This active management consists of determining which data to forward next, which data to store for forwarding later, and which data to drop.
  * 2\. The enforcement of service level agreements through the selective acceptance of traffic into a node \(or network\) based on pre-determined criteria. Again, this acceptance is based on determining which data to accept now, which data to store for acceptance later and which data to deny \(drop\).
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> What is Quality of Service?
text_preview:
1. A mechanism to manage data transmission when a link approaches saturation: deciding what to forward, store, or drop.
2. Enforcing service level agreements by selectively accepting traffic based on pre-determined criteria: deciding what to accept, store, or deny.

trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> What is Quality of Service?

text: Fundamentally, QoS only operates when traffic is flowing at the limits of capacity \(either physical or logical\). When flowing traffic rates are well below the limits, QoS is essentially benign allowing all traffic to be forwarded as it is received.
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> What is Quality of Service?

text: Why do we need QoS?
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> Why do we need QoS?
text_preview: Why do we need QoS?

text: Applications using the network transport will often require certain capabilities from the network in
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> Why do we need QoS?
text_preview: Applications using the network transport will often require certain capabilities from the network in

text: order for the application to function correctly.
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> Why do we need QoS?
text_preview: order for the application to function correctly.

trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> Why do we need QoS?
24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> Why do we need QoS?
text_preview:
Real-time voice services, such as telephone calls, have a maximum latency threshold before interactive speech becomes difficult. This translates to two demands from the network:

1. Minimising hop-by-hop latency for voice packets.
2. Minimising packet jitter to reduce de-jitter buffer latency at the receiver.

text: It is useful then to be able to identify voice traffic in the network and prioritise if for forwarding such that it is not held up behind other less time sensitive traffic.
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> Why do we need QoS?
text_preview: It is useful then to be able to identify voice traffic in the network and prioritise if for forwarding such that it is not held up behind other less time sensitive traffic.

text: A second example might be an Electronic Point of Sale \(EPoS\) application. This type of application does not need to be particularly latency bound \(a few 10s or 100s of milliseconds in packet arrival does not impact the service\), but it does need to have some guaranteed capacity in order to function. I.e. we do not want the EPoS application struggling for bandwidth because a large data transfer is taking place. This guaranteed bandwidth requirement also translates into network demands.
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> Why do we need QoS?
text_preview: An Electronic Point of Sale (EPoS) application doesn't need low latency, but it requires guaranteed capacity to function. A large data transfer shouldn't impact the service or cause bandwidth issues. This requirement translates into network demands.

text:
* 1\. Minimising packet loss for the traffic, if necessary, storing it locally until the local egress interface has capacity to send it on.
  * 2\. Reserving a minimum amount of transmission time \(or bandwidth\) on the interface for packets of the EPoS application.
trace: 24 Annex D: Quality of Service --> Why do we need QoS?
text_preview:
* 1\. Minimising packet loss for the traffic, if necessary, storing it locally until the local egress interface has capacity to send it on.
  * 2\. Reserving a minimum amount of transmission time \(or bandwidth\) on the interface for packets of the EPoS application.

text: QoS then is the mechanism by which operators can identify applications in an infrastructure and apply policies to the infrastructure to maintain the applications transport requirements, even when capacity is limited.

text: In this model, traffic arriving at a node is classified, \(allocated to some internal category\) based on the context associated with its arrival. For example, it might be assumed that all traffic arriving from a specific logical or physical interface will be categorized as "best effort". This specific example actually represents the default behaviour for almost all network elements, and is useful to recognise, as it forms the basis for all other classifications. I.e. that without further modification, traffic arriving at a node will be treated as best effort \(without any specific explicit treatment\).

text: Traffic marking

text: As described above, a key attribute of a QoS architecture is the ability to pass information about the QoS status of a packet between nodes, and indeed within a node \(e.g. from ingress to egress\). This is achieved through the use of QoS markings, setting bit fields within a packet header that convey some information about the QoS related context in which this packet should be considered.
trace: --> Traffic classification and marking --> Traffic marking
text_preview: A key attribute of a QoS architecture is passing packet QoS status between nodes and within a node (e.g., from ingress to egress). This is achieved through QoS markings, setting bit fields in a packet header that convey QoS context information.

text: Again, as described above there are numerous traffic marking schemes that are in use, each associated with a particular header type in the packet \(or frame\) world. There are also bit fields defined in meta-data associated with internal forwarding in many router and switch silicon architectures. Two examples of this are "Discard Class or Loss Priority" often associated with the output of a policing function, but also explicitly settable, and "qos-group" or "forwarding-class", an opaque field provided in many router implementations
trace: --> Traffic classification and marking --> Traffic marking

Bit fields in meta-data facilitate internal forwarding in routers and switches. Examples include "Discard Class or Loss Priority" and "qos-group", which are settable by policing function and opaque field respectively.

text: The use and meaning associated with the values represented by these bits is entirely arbitrary, as defined and used by users and operators. However, the value in their use lies in having agreed meaning that can be passed between network elements. Some fields, for example IP DSCP, have recommend meanings that can be used between providers. Others, such as MPLS TC \(EXP\) are not formally defined so as to remain flexible.

text: Congestion management
trace: --> Traffic classification and marking --> Congestion management
text_preview: Congestion management

text: Thus far we have discussed the options available for classifying traffic. But once classified, we must consider what behaviour to apply. As mentioned in the introduction to this section, a QoS node fundamentally only has three options available for managing traffic; forward, store for forwarding later or drop, but these options need only be applied when a bandwidth resource is congested.
trace: --> Traffic classification and marking --> Congestion management
text_preview: We've discussed traffic classification options. Once classified, we must consider behavior to apply. A QoS node has 3 fundamental options: forward, store for later, or drop - which are only needed when bandwidth is congested.

trace: --> Traffic classification and marking --> Congestion management

text: A key function of QoS is that of managing traffic during congestion of an interface. Congestion occurs when the quantity of traffic to be forwarded on an interface exceeds its capacity. In its simplest form, QoS alleviates this issue by buffering the excess traffic, i.e. storing it in a local memory until such time that the interface is available to send the stored traffic.
trace: --> Traffic classification and marking --> Congestion management
text_preview: QoS manages traffic during congestion of an interface. Congestion occurs when traffic exceeds capacity. In its simplest form, QoS alleviates this issue by buffering excess traffic in local memory until the interface is available to send it.

text: FIFO Queueing
trace: --> FIFO Queueing
text_preview: FIFO Queueing

text: By storing packets that need to be sent on to this interface in the order they arrive, and then sending them in that order when the interface is free, we form a "first in - first out" \(FIFO\) queue of packets.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing
text_preview: By storing packets that need to be sent on to this interface in the order they arrive, and then sending them in that order when the interface is free, we form a "first in - first out" \(FIFO\) queue of packets.

trace: --> FIFO Queueing

text: This mechanism, queueing, is a useful tool for managing temporary congestion, smoothing out the bursts of traffic flowing into an interface, and forms the basis for more complex congestion management tools.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing
text_preview: This mechanism, queueing, is a useful tool for managing temporary congestion, smoothing out the bursts of traffic flowing into an interface, and forms the basis for more complex congestion management tools.

text: There are four aspects of this capability that cause challenges;
trace: --> FIFO Queueing
text_preview: There are four aspects of this capability that cause challenges;

text:
* 1\. By storing traffic for later sending, we intrinsically delay that traffic that is being stored, adding latency to the transmission path for that traffic. Further, because the delay may be variable, \(different amounts of traffic may be enqueued prior to this packet arriving\) we introduce jitter.
  * 2\. As the speeds of the interfaces we are managing increases, we need more memory capacity to store enough packets to substantively impact the traffic we are buffering.
  * 3\. The process is of queuing traffic is indiscriminate, in that it impacts all traffic flowing through an interface. This presents the same latency implication to all applications using this interface, some of which will be impacted by this delay, and some will not.
  * 4\. As the amount of memory available to for the queue is finite, so the queue is finite. As a result, if the rate of arrival of traffic to be forwarded is significantly higher than the interface rate or the burst is long enough, the available buffer will be filled, and no further traffic can be enqueued. At this point, the node has no option but to drop traffic. When a queue is full, and a node can no longer add packets to the end \(tail\) of the queue, traffic otherwise destined for that queue is indiscriminately dropped from the tail \(tail drop\), until such time that the queue depth reduces and space is made available again for new traffic.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing
text_preview:
Storing traffic for later sending introduces latency and jitter due to variable delay.
As interface speeds increase, more memory capacity is needed to store packets.
Queuing traffic impacts all applications equally, causing latency.
Dropping traffic leads to tail drop, where packets are dropped from the end of the queue.

text: It is worth remembering at this point that the application of QoS to an infrastructure is only a solution for the management of how traffic is dropped under congestion conditions. It is not a replacement for capacity planning and management for traffic that MUST be delivered. I.e. if a network has less capacity available than the amount of traffic that MUST be delivered, applying QoS is not an alternative to augmenting the capacity.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing
text_preview: Applying Quality of Service (QoS) to infrastructure only addresses how traffic is dropped under congestion conditions. It's not a replacement for capacity planning and management for guaranteed traffic delivery. If a network can't deliver all required traffic due to capacity constraints, QoS isn't an alternative to increasing capacity.

text: However, it is possible to significantly improve on this single FIFO queue model by combining the use of classification with a programable scheduler to determine how we enqueue traffic, how much we allow to pass, and what to do with the excess.

text: By combining the concept of classifying traffic with the concept of a queue it is possible to allow a node to manage the traffic flowing on an interface with a behaviour that is appropriate to the applications flowing in each class.

text: In this model, shown in Figure 24-4, the system identifies separate logical queues for traffic destined to flow out of a given interface. Traffic can be placed into a queue based on the classification information gained on arrival \(or if the system is capable, after the packet has been forwarded – determined that it should flow out of this specific interface\).

text: For example, traffic identified as needing low latency, and low jitter \(real time – our voice calls from earlier\) may be placed into queue 1. Traffic requiring some minimum bandwidth \(business critical, our EPOS traffic\) may be placed into queue 3. Traffic that has no specific requirements \(best effort\) may be placed into queue 5.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Class based queueing
text_preview:
Traffic with low latency and jitter (real-time voice calls) goes to queue 1.
Business-critical traffic requiring minimum bandwidth goes to queue 3.
Best-effort traffic with no specific requirements goes to queue 5.

text: The scheduler can now be programmed to dequeue traffic and place it onto the interface following a pre-determined policy – for example;
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Class based queueing
text_preview: The scheduler can now be programmed to dequeue traffic and place it onto the interface following a pre-determined policy – for example;

text:
* 1\. Serve all high-priority traffic first \(E.g. Queue 1 and 2\), up to a given capacity of the interface for each queue \(for example 50% and 5%\). Any traffic arriving at this interface for those queues that cannot be served at that rate should be placed into the appropriate queue.
  * 2\. Serve traffic from low priority queues \(queue 3, 4 and 5\) with equal priority \(a packet from each\) until the minimum guaranteed amount of bandwidth allocated to that queue is met.
  * 3\. Continue to serve traffic from low priority queues until either the queue is empty, or the interface bandwidth is consumed.

* Serve high-priority traffic (Queues 1 & 2) up to 50% and 5% capacity, respectively.
* Serve low-priority traffic (Queues 3-5) with equal priority until minimum guaranteed bandwidth is met for each queue.
* Continue serving low-priority queues until empty or interface bandwidth is consumed.

text: Admission control
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Admission control
text_preview: Admission control

text: This is the process of managing the amount of traffic that we accept into the network. This can be thought of as the enforcement of the contract between the applications requirements', and the networks transport capability. Returning to the example of the voice call, let us imagine that the transport network has enough capacity to sustain 100 concurrent voice calls \(Figure 24-6\). If more than 100 calls are introduced there is insufficient bandwidth to sustain all the calls and some traffic will inevitably be dropped. Because the dropping of traffic will be random, all calls will be impacted by the packet loss equally, resulting in reduced voice quality or even call failure.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Admission control
text_preview: Managing network traffic involves enforcing the contract between app requirements and network transport capacity. If a transport network can handle 100 concurrent voice calls, introducing more than that leads to insufficient bandwidth, causing some traffic to be dropped. This results in packet loss, impacting all calls equally, leading to reduced voice quality or call failure.

text: By pre-agreeing that the network can only sustain a certain number of calls, we can police the traffic arriving from the application, to the agreed level. In the case of the packet network, this means agreeing a sustainable bandwidth level and honouring that level at the point that we accept traffic from the application.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Admission control
text_preview: By pre-agreeing that the network can only sustain a certain number of calls, we can police the traffic arriving from the application, to the agreed level. In the case of the packet network, this means agreeing a sustainable bandwidth level and honouring that level at the point that we accept traffic from the application.

text: Once we have classified traffic to determine that it is indeed voice traffic, we can apply a policer to that traffic class to limit the amount of traffic that is accepted. If the application violates the agreed rate, the policer will drop some packets, forwarding only the rate that was previously agreed. It should be noted that for this particular application, again voice quality will suffer, however, the onus is now on the application to stay within the terms of the agreed contract for the benefit of its own service.

This will negatively impact voice quality, but the onus falls on the application to adhere to the contract for its own service.

text: So, if by dropping traffic at admission to the network we will see the application service degrade, just as if we drop traffic in the middle of the network, why bother? Should we not simply let the traffic have access and hope there is sufficient capacity to support the application demand?

text: This is where the network level administration of QoS becomes relevant. Consider the same core network resource now being shared by two customers \(Figure 24-7\). If we recognise that the network can only sustain 100 calls, we can ask each customer to restrict their usage, customer 1 to 60 calls and customer 2 to 40 calls. By applying a policy that is specific to each customer context we can ensure that the available network resources are not exhausted, resulting in poor performance for all.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Admission control
text_preview: At the network level, QoS administration becomes relevant when two customers share the same core network resource (\(Figure 24-7\)). If the network can only sustain 100 calls, we can restrict each customer's usage: 60 calls for customer 1 and 40 calls for customer 2.

text: If customer 1 exceeds their allocated capacity, some traffic will be dropped at point 1, resulting in poor quality for customer 1. However, if customer 2 continues to maintain their agreement not to exceed 40 calls, there will always be sufficient capacity to support their service without quality impairment.
