text: Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
text_preview: Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)

text: When looking at congestion management, the idea of a queue was introduced in order to store traffic that is awaiting transmission on an outgoing interface. In this previous discussion we saw that in a simple queue, when the queue is full, any additional traffic is "tail dropped" indiscriminately.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
text_preview: When looking at congestion management, the idea of a queue was introduced in order to store traffic that is awaiting transmission on an outgoing interface. In this previous discussion we saw that in a simple queue, when the queue is full, any additional traffic is "tail dropped" indiscriminately.

text: For applications that are using a TCP connection over IP, the loss of one \(or more\) packets from the flow will cause the TCP algorithm to time out and request re-delivery of these missing packets. This also triggers the shortening of the TCP "ack window" resulting in lower throughput for that TCP session. As many TCP session may be impacted at once in a tail drop scenario, this can cause a number of sessions to "back off" reducing the total load on the interface, and the queue to be drained.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
text_preview: For applications using TCP over IP, packet loss triggers timeout and re-delivery requests. This shortens the "ack window", reducing throughput for affected sessions. In a tail drop scenario, multiple sessions may back off, draining the queue and reducing interface load.

text: Over time, the TCP sessions will re-open their ACK window, increasing bandwidth until the interface is once again full and the queue overwhelmed. The result is a sawtooth type bandwidth profile that oscillates around the maximum interface speed. This oscillation reduces the efficiency of the interface usage as there are periods where the interface is not full.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
text_preview: Over time, the TCP sessions will re-open their ACK window, increasing bandwidth until the interface is once again full and the queue overwhelmed. The result is a sawtooth type bandwidth profile that oscillates around the maximum interface speed. This oscillation reduces the efficiency of the interface usage as there are periods where the interface is not full.

text: Weighted Random early discard \(WRED\) is a modification to the queue drop behaviour that can help to eliminate this effect. The premise is to manage the acceptance of traffic into the queue in a more intelligent manner.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
text_preview: Weighted Random early discard \(WRED\) is a modification to the queue drop behaviour that can help to eliminate this effect. The premise is to manage the acceptance of traffic into the queue in a more intelligent manner.

text: Figure 24-8: RED queue threshold
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)

text: Consider the queue in Figure 24-8, with three depths at 0% \(1\), 50% \(2\) and 100 % \(3\). As traffic arrives for the interface and the scheduler has no capacity available to forward them, the waiting packets are placed into the queue. Between queue depth 1 \(0% full\) and depth 2 \(50% full\), packets are added as normal to the queue.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
text_preview: In Figure 24-8, a queue has three depths: 0%, 50%, and 100%. When traffic arrives, waiting packets fill the queue if space is available. Packets between depth 1 (0%) and depth 2 (50%) are added normally.

text: When the queue depth reaches the lower RED threshold \(2\) \(50% in this example\), rather than adding all new packets to the queue, some will be randomly dropped. The probability of dropping any given packet changes dependent on the current \(and possibly historical\) queue depth. As the depth of the queue increases, so does the probability of drop until at depth 3 \(100% full\) the probability of drop is 1 \(always drop\).
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
text_preview:
When the queue depth reaches the lower RED threshold (2, 50%), packets are randomly dropped instead of being added to the queue. The drop probability increases with depth:

- Depth 1: <50%
- Depth 3 (100% full): always drop

text: The impact of this weighted behaviour is to slowly encourage individual TCP sessions flowing in the queue to find an appropriate TCP window \(and hence bandwidth\) such that the queue never saturates, and the link can continue flowing at 100% capacity, eliminating the sawtooth behaviour.
trace: --> FIFO Queueing --> Weighted Random Early Discard \(WRED\)
text_preview: The impact of this weighted behaviour is to slowly encourage individual TCP sessions flowing in the queue to find an appropriate TCP window \(and hence bandwidth\) such that the queue never saturates, and the link can continue flowing at 100% capacity, eliminating the sawtooth behaviour.

text: We have seen it is possible to add traffic to a specific queue based on a classification, in order to differentiate between traffic types flowing in an interface. This allows us the flexibility to manage bandwidth to support different applications in an infrastructure. We have also seen that under some circumstances it might be possible to "borrow" bandwidth from one class to use in another class, in the event that the bandwidth in an interface is not fully used.

text_preview: We've seen it's possible to add traffic to a specific queue based on classification, allowing us to manage bandwidth for different applications. In some cases, we can "borrow" unused bandwidth from one class to support another, even if the interface isn't fully utilized.

text: It is possible to extend the idea differentiated behaviour for traffic from between queues, to within a single queue using the Weighted RED scheme.

text: It should be noted that the PE is not policing "sessions", but simply the traffic associated with those sessions. The PE has no knowledge of the nature of the traffic sent by the CE \(for example the membership of a specific packet to a specific session\), other than the markings being examined. It should also be noted that traffic dropped at point \(3\) will contain packets associated with many or all of the sessions from the CE whose traffic is being marked "out-of-contract". The impact of this is that all TCP sessions that lose traffic will again contract their TCP windows, with the effect of lowering the BW used by each session and so reducing the load on the network.

text_preview: The PE doesn't police "sessions", but only the associated traffic. It has no knowledge of packet membership beyond markings. Traffic dropped at point 3 will contain packets from multiple sessions marked as "out-of-contract". This leads to TCP sessions losing traffic, contracting their windows, lowering bandwidth usage, and reducing network load.

Compare this to the example in Service protection through admission control where the network resource at point 3 may be under used.

text: PIM-based overlay signalling for IPVPN
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> PIM-based overlay signalling for IPVPN
text_preview: PIM-based overlay signalling for IPVPN

text: The most straightforward way is to emulate a per-VPN pseudo LAN over the underlay network. The pseudo LAN is instantiated by a multicast GRE tunnel for the VPN. Every PE for the VPN joins that tunnel and can send both control plane \(PIM messages\) and data plane traffic over the tunnel. For example, multicast group 225.1.1.1 used for VPN1, 225.1.1.2 for VPN2, etc.
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> PIM-based overlay signalling for IPVPN
text_preview: The most straightforward way is to emulate a per-VPN pseudo LAN by using a multicast GRE tunnel over the underlay network. Every PE joins this tunnel and sends both control plane (PIM messages) and data plane traffic through it, using multicast groups like 225.1.1.1 for VPNs.

text: This is referred to as PIM-MVPN and also commonly as Rosen-MVPN. It is documented in the historic RFC6037 and further in RFC6513 \[119\] \(which documents both PIM- and BGP-based overlay signaling\).
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> PIM-based overlay signalling for IPVPN
text_preview: This is referred to as PIM-MVPN and also commonly as Rosen-MVPN. It is documented in the historic RFC6037 and further in RFC6513 \[119\] \(which documents both PIM- and BGP-based overlay signaling\).

text: Essentially, a PE runs PIM sessions over each pseudo LAN for each VPN. This is different from unicast, with which no per-VPN session is used.
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> PIM-based overlay signalling for IPVPN
text_preview: Essentially, a PE runs PIM sessions over each pseudo LAN for each VPN. This is different from unicast, with which no per-VPN session is used.

text: When there are a large number of VPNs, many PIM sessions and signalling \(including message refreshes\) are incurred so it does not scale well. Most implementations and deployments of PIM/Rosen-MVPN only use IP multicast tunnel in the underlay to emulate the pseudo LANs.

  * Multicast \(IP\) VPN with BGP based overlay signalling is referred to BGP-MVPN. While RFC6513\[119\] covers both PIM-MVPN and BGP-MVPN concepts, BGP-MVPN specific encoding and procedures are specified in RFC6514 \[120\] .

text: As mentioned above, overlay multicast traffic is transported via underlay multicast tunnels. Many tunnel types have been mature and widely deployed, but with Segment Routing and central control being widely adopted, it is necessary to review the pros and cons of various multicast technologies and see what is the best solution in the SR era.

Many tunnel types have been mature and widely deployed, but with Segment Routing and central control being widely adopted, it is necessary to review the pros and cons of various multicast technologies and see what is the best solution in the SR era.

text: Traditionally, multicast requires per-tree state on all routers of a tree for efficient replication. PIM, RSVP-TE P2MP, mLDP P2MP/MP2MP are all signaling protocols to instantiate tree state on those routers, either from the tree leaves towards the tree root or vice versa. The new SR-P2MP \(aka tree- sid\) tunnels also requires per-tree state on all root/leaf and replication nodes, except that the signalling is directly from a central controller who also calculates the tree.

text: Obviously, this does not go well with one principal of Segment Routing – no per-flow state inside the network. An alternative is Ingress Replication – the root tunnels individual copies directly to leaves so no per-tree state is needed inside the network. Since replication is done at the root, it is not efficient and does not work well for high fan-out hight data rate cases.

text_preview: One principal of Segment Routing doesn't go well with per-flow state inside the network. An alternative is Ingress Replication, where individual copies are sent directly to leaves, eliminating the need for per-tree state. However, this approach is inefficient and not suitable for high fan-out, high data rate cases.

trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> Underlay multicast

text: BIER \(RFC8279 \[132\], RFC8296 \[134\]\) is a new technology that achieves efficient replication w/o incurring per-tree state, so it is the ideal multicast solution for an SR network. However, it uses a new encapsulation and forwarding algorithm, so it requires new hardware. While this makes it difficult to deploy in non-greenfield networks, there are very well-designed brownfield deployment methods, and all major vendors have BIER implementation & hardware available/upcoming.
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> Underlay multicast
text_preview: BIER (\[RFC8279\], \[RFC8296\]) is a multicast solution for SR networks that achieves efficient replication without per-tree state. It uses new encapsulation and forwarding algorithms requiring new hardware, but well-designed brownfield methods are available from major vendors.

trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> Underlay multicast

text: For an SR network, an operator may prefer to remove all legacy multicast signaling – PIM/RSVP/mLDP and switch to controller-based tree calculation and signaling via either PCEP or BGP \(i.e., SR-P2MP \[draft-ietf-pim-sr-p2mp-policy\[173\]\] \[draft-ietf-spring-sr-replication-segment\] or BGP-signaled IP/MPLS multicast \[draft-ietf-bess-bgp-multicast-controller\[160\]\]\). Notice that this still incurs per-tree state inside the network and the only real benefit is the central calculation of the tree based on many TE constraints/considerations.

text: Given the vast scale of the transport network, a seamless architecture is used as described previously. In this architecture, two aspects have impacts to multicast:
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> Underlay multicast --> MVPN/EVPN and Seamless MPLS/SR
text_preview: Given the vast scale of the transport network, a seamless architecture is used as described previously. In this architecture, two aspects have impacts to multicast:

text:
* a\) Only border routes have routes to edges nodes \(that connect to 5G NFs like RAN/UPF\), while internal routers only have routes to the border routes.
  * b\) Different ASes/areas may support/prefer different types of underlay tunnels
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> Underlay multicast --> MVPN/EVPN and Seamless MPLS/SR
text_preview:
* a\) Only border routes have routes to edges nodes \(that connect to 5G NFs like RAN/UPF\), while internal routers only have routes to the border routes.
  * b\) Different ASes/areas may support/prefer different types of underlay tunnels

text: For a\), to establish end-to-end underlay tunnels across those different ASes/areas, PIM RPF vector \[RFC5496\]\[109\] or mLDP Recursive FEC \[RFC6512\]\[118\] can be used – a leaf router looks up the route to the tree root, with the BGP protocol nexthop being a border router in the local area/AS. It then encodes that border router's address in PIM/mLDP signaling so that internal routers will signal towards that border router instead of the original root. When that border router gets the signaling, it encodes the next border router's address so that the internal routers in the next AS/area will signal towards the next border router, and so on so forth.
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> Underlay multicast --> MVPN/EVPN and Seamless MPLS/SR
text_preview: to establish underlay tunnels across different ases , use pim rpf vector ( rfc 5 4 9 6 ) or mldp recursive fec ( rfc 6 5 1 2 ). a leaf router looks up the tree root using bgp protocol nexthop as a border router in its local area / as . it then encodes this address

text: An alternative solution for a\) is use controller signaled multicast, since the routers become dumb forwarding devices programed with forwarding state for the tunnels by the controllers.
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> Underlay multicast --> MVPN/EVPN and Seamless MPLS/SR
text_preview: An alternative solution for a\) is use controller signaled multicast, since the routers become dumb forwarding devices programed with forwarding state for the tunnels by the controllers.

text: For b\), MVPN/EVPN-BUM tunnel segmentation RFC7524 \[123\] and draft-ietf-bess-bgp-multicast- controller \[168\] can be used – MVPN/EVPN-BUM procedures will run on the border routers and the signaled tunnel type/identification are changed as MVPN/EVPN routes are re-advertised by the border routers, so that different tunnel types/instances are used in different ASes/areas.
trace: 25 Annex E: Multicast Technologies background --> Underlay multicast --> MVPN/EVPN and Seamless MPLS/SR
text_preview: For b\), RFC7524 and draft-ietf-bess-bgp-multicast-controller can be used – MVPN/EVPN-BUM procedures run on border routers, using different tunnel types/instances based on signaled tunnel type/identification.

text: WG-1 is developing a slicing architecture contained in O-RAN.WG1.Slicing-Architecture-v07.00 \[25\]. It is a multi-phased effort based on the roadmaps of the different O-RAN working groups combined with use cases specified by O-RAN operators. The use cases are additive, so a slicing phase 2 environment must be able to concurrently support phase 1 and phase 2 use cases.
trace: 26 Annex F: Transport network slicing solution for WG1 Slicing \(informational\)
text_preview: WG-1 is developing a slicing architecture in O-RAN. It's a multi-phased effort combining roadmaps from different working groups with operator-specific use cases. The architecture supports additive use cases, requiring a phase 2 environment to coexist with phases 1 and 2.

text: This annex currently addresses the transport network solution needed to support the use cases in phase 1 and 2 of WG-1's slicing architecture \[25\]. There are potentially many ways a packet switched network can address the requirements outlined by WG-1, so this section has been presented as an example solution that uses capabilities defined in the main body of this document. This annex is inline with work done by IETF TEAS WG in draft-ietf-teas-5g-ns-ip-mpls dealing with a realization of IETF network slices for 5G networks using current IP/MPLS technologies \(\[179\]\).

text_preview: This annex addresses transport network solution support for phase 1 & 2 WG-1 slicing architecture requirements. It presents an example solution using capabilities defined in this document, aligning with IETF TEAS WG work on 5G network slices (draft-ietf-teas-5g-ns-ip-mpls).

trace: 26 Annex F: Transport network slicing solution for WG1 Slicing \(informational\) --> WG-1 Phase 1 scope
text_preview: Not illustrated in Figure 26-1, the following has been assumed or are limitations in slicing phase 1.

text:
* The transport network is multi-service and in addition to 5G needs to support:
  * o 3G and 4G mobile services
  * o Wireline services \(consumer, enterprise, and wholesale\)
  * Mobile components connect directly to the transport network or reside in a data centre that connects to the transport network.
  * O-RAN and 3GPP components present slices to the transport network or Data Center infrastructure via a discrete physical or logical Ethernet interface \(VLANs\).
  * Data Centers, connected to the transport network, present slices to the transport network via logical Ethernet interfaces \(VLANs\).
  * There is no slicing in phase 1 in Fronthaul and Midhaul due to lack of slicing support in these mobile components.
  * For the transport network to support QoS appropriate to the QoS requirements of the mobile infrastructure, it is necessary for the O-RAN and 3GPP mobile components, in the Midhaul and Backhaul, to set the DSCP bits in the IP header of the GTP-U packets based on the importance of the user's traffic in the radio domain. In slicing phase 1 this is possible for Uplink and Downlink traffic in Backhaul but only for Downlink traffic in Midhaul.
  * No multicast capability in required in slicing phase 1.
  * Management architectures and interfaces to packet switched infrastructure for slicing are dealt with in O-RAN.WG9.XTRP-MGT.0-v04.00 "Management interfaces for Transport Network Elements v04.00", July 2022\[23\]

  * Enterprise Core Slice: Slices for enterprise customers where the enterprise's UPF is located centrally.
  * Enterprise Private Cloud Slice \#1 and \#2: Slices for enterprise customers where the enterprise's UPFs are in central and distributed locations. Two examples are shown; 1\) UPFs are sited in either the RAN cluster PoP or the Collector Rural Mid PoP and the Core DC Central PoP. In this instance all UPFs share common backhaul and N6 networks. 2\) UPFs are sited in Regional Zone Big PoP and the Core DC Central PoP. In this case their N6 networks are discrete logical networks.

text: It is a converged end to end packet switched infrastructure, beginning at the cell site, located in the edge of the access layer, and stretching to the core of the transport layer. The packet switching TNEs are IP/MPLS or SRv6, QoS enabled, high capacity, low latency devices interconnected by point-to-point Ethernet interfaces running at the full capacity of the Ethernet interface, typically using either point to point fibres or via a WDM infrastructure. It incorporates data centers suitably placed across the transport network infrastructure to support virtual and physical NFs associated with mobile and fixed services but also potentially the placement of "Application Functions" associated with value-add services and customer specific application.

text: A packet switched network has extensive capabilities to support slicing. These are outlined in section 18. Slicing phase 1 is basic in nature with limited slicing capabilities in the O-RAN mobile components and the actual slices \(mobile BB, MMTc, NB-IOT\) are low priority and delay tolerant slices. In phase 2, some additional slice types are added \(MBB IPTV, Enterprise Core, Enterprise Private Cloud\), with more distributed 3GPP, O-RAN component and Application Functions \(UPFs and CDNs can be located at regional and central DC levels\), and more – but still not very critical – delay sensitivity \(for example IPTV\). Phase 3 adds even distribution possibilities. With this in mind, and more onerous slicing use cases in later phases, it is proposed to support slicing phase 1 and 2 in the transport network using:
trace: Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3
text_preview: A packet switched network supports extensive slicing capabilities (section 18). Phases 1 & 2 add slice types like MMTc and NB-IOT, with Phase 3 enabling even distribution possibilities. To support phases 1-2, the transport network uses return paths for slicing.

text:
* Default IGP instances running in each underlay routing domain calculating shortest path routing based on IGP metrics.
  * IGP supporting fast and loop free convergence.
  * Inter-domain connectivity performed using either BGP, IGP redistributing or a PCE infrastructure.
  * Management, control and user planes in phase 1 and 2 use shortest path routing between TNEs. I.e., the Service VPNs associated with each slice are not mapped to TE tunnels or Flex-algos in phase 1 or 2.

text: As the WG-1 slicing use cases and slicing capabilities within O-RAN equipment matures so more sophisticated forwarding techniques, such as SR-TE and Flex-algo may need to be utilised. Therefore, phase 3 introduces mapping between Service VPNs and transport planes, where each transport plane is realized via set of tunnels optimized for some common characteristics. For example, one transport plane could reflect set of tunnels optimized for latency \(using latency link metrics for optimization\), where another transport plane could group tunnels optimized for high capacity \(but not necessarily low latency\), using IGP metrics. Tunnels could be TE tunnels \(RSVP, SR-TE, SRv6-TE\), or different Flex-Algos. This approach might result in different path being taken by different slices. Please see Section 18.1 "Packet-switched underlay network" for discussion on how they can be applied and used to support slicing.

text: Transport network management network
trace: Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Service Models for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Transport and DC management networks --> Transport network management network
text_preview: Transport network management network

text: A network wide in-band L3VPN is used for day-to-day management of the TNEs. Every TNE has a local network management interface with an associated network management IP address configured at installation. This is typically a loopback interface. Management protocols associated with TNE's configuration, monitoring and service orchestration are configured to use this interface as their source interface. The TNE's management interface is placed into a transport management network built using a MP-BGP L3VPN mapped to the underlay's default routing algorithm. The transport network management network can be designed as an any-to-any network, meaning that every entity within the L3VPN can connect to every other entity in the transport network management network but are more commonly built so that the central network management functions can communicate with the TNEs and vice versa but the TNEs cannot communicate with each other. In addition to the in-band management network Service Providers may also choose to have an out- of-band network for scenarios when in-band network connectivity has been lost. Various solutions exist, often based on access to the console port, through mobile, xDSL or PON technology.

text: In the packet switched transport architecture data centers are distributed around the transport network and although distributed they need to be managed centrally. The DC infrastructure supports "Network Functions" and "Applications Functions". Some functions are associated with the provision of 5G and O-RAN capabilities and services, but DCs should be considered common infrastructure facilities that support services beyond just 5G. The DC management network needs to support the O2 interface defined by O-RAN but also other data center management, monitoring and orchestration facilities. In the slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 the handoff between the DC and the transport network is via a logical Ethernet attachment circuit. The design of the management infrastructure within the DC is handled by WG-6, with connectivity between DCs and the central DC management infrastructure provided by the transport network. Each DC needs to hand-off the DC management network to a TNE via a logical Ethernet interface. On the TNE the logical Ethernet attachment circuit is placed into a MP-BGP L3VPN mapped to the underlay's default routing algorithm. text: Based on guidance from WG-1, the O-RAN Fronthaul M-Plane interface is supported across the transport network as a dedicated VPN. This is discrete from the O-RAN Management and Control VPN that supports the O-RAN A1, E2 and O1 interfaces. The reasoning is Fronthaul management and O-RAN control and management may fall under different organizations within the Service Provider.

This separation is due to differing organizational structures within Service Providers.

text: Full details of Fronthaul M-plane can be found in section 7.1. The design outlined assumes the Fronthaul M-plane is operating in hybrid mode, where a central Fronthaul NMS needs IP connectivity to the O-DUs and the O-RUs. The O-RAN Fronthaul Management network in the transport network uses a MP-BGP L3VPN mapped to the underlay's default routing algorithm. The VPN needs to be present on all TNEs, through VLAN attachment circuits, that support O-RAN mobile components managed using the Fronthaul M-Plane. O-RAN mobile components that use the M-Plane need to connect to the O-RAN Fronthaul Management VPN, via a logical Ethernet interface, when they are installed or instantiated.

text:
* Near-Real-Time RIC \(Near-RT RIC\). Near-RT RICs use the E2 interface to communicate with the O-CUs, and O-DUs they control. The interface controls the O-CUs and O-DUs with execution actions coming from the Near-RT RIC and feedback in the opposite direction.
  * Non-Real-Time RIC \(Non-RT RIC\). Non-RT RICs use the A1 interface to communicate with the Near-RT RICs they control. The interface provides the Near-RT RICs with policies, enrichment info, and ML model updates. In the other direction the Near-RT RICs provides policy feedback to the Non-RT RIC.
  * The O1 interface is associated with "Service and Management Orchestration". This interface is an FCAPs interface with configuration, registration, security, performance, and monitoring responsibilities.
  * The O-RAN Control and Management network in the transport network uses MP-BGP L3VPN technology, mapped to the underlay's default routing algorithm. It needs to be present on all TNEs through VLAN attachment circuits, that support O-RAN components that use either the A1, E2 or O1 interfaces. All O-RAN components using these interfaces need to connect, via the TNEs, to the O-RAN Management and Control VPN when they are installed or instantiated.
  * The O-RAN control and management VPN can be designed as an any-to-any network, meaning that every O-RAN component in the L3VPN can connect to any other entity in the O-RAN control and management VPN, or more likely built as a tiered VPN using a combination of Virtual Routing and Forwarding \(VRFs\) instances and Route Targets \(RTs\) so that:
  * SMO can communicate Near-RT RICs, O-CU-CPs, O-CU-UPs and O-DUs.
  * Non-RT RIC can communicate with the Near-RT RICs.
  * Near-RT RICs can communicate with the O-CUs, O-DUs and O-RUs.

text:
* In slicing phase 1 slicing is not supported on Midhaul O-RAN mobile components. O-DUs and O-
  * CU-UPs do not have a concept of slicing with the F1-U traffic from all slices originating and
  * terminating on the same physical/logical interface and IP address on the O-DU. In scenarios, where
  * the O-CU-UP is shared between two or more slices there is also no concept of slicing on the O-CU-
  * UP. In situations, as shown in Figure 26-2, where the O-CU-UP is dedicated to a slice, then the O-
  * CU-UP function will only receive and send traffic associated with that slice, however the O-CU-UP
  * slice assignment and selection process is completely transparent to the transport network and under
  * the control of the O-RAN / 3GPP control planes. For this reason, in slicing phase 1 a single MP-
  * BGP L3VPN mapped to the underlay's default routing algorithm is used across the transport
  * network to support all Midhaul user plane traffic regardless of slice it belongs too. The L3VPN
  * needs to be present on all TNEs and DC-TNEs that either connect directly or indirectly \(through the
  * DC infrastructure\) to mobile components that support Midhaul user plane interfaces. Access to the
  * Midhaul user plane VPN, on the TNEs, is via VLAN interfaces.
  * A further challenge with Midhaul user plane interfaces in slicing phase 1 is the lack of a QoS
  * mapping function on the O-DUs to map radio orientated QoS parameters, controlled by the 3GPP /
  * ORAN control planes, to transport orientated DSCP QoS markings. The means the transport
  * network QoS mechanisms must treat all uplink traffic the same, regardless of the importance of the
  * data contained within Midhaul GTP-U packets.
  * Slicing Phase 2 and 3
  * Midhaul slicing and QoS is supported in slicing phase 2 and 3. F1-U traffic segregation is supported
  * using a VLAN per user plane slice on the O-DUs and O-CU-UPs and QoS is supported by the O-
  * DUs and O-CU-UPs setting a DSCP value appropriate to the importance of the user payload in the
  * GTP-U packet.

text: A full description of MP-BGP based L3VPNs is contained in sections 13.3 and Annex C: MP-BGP  based L3VPNs. MP-BGP based L3VPNs support flexible connectivity models and are highly scalable in terms of sites, VPNs and the number of VPN IP routes so able to deal with transport connectivity requirements associated with WG-1s slicing phases and the anticipated size of 5G environments. MP-BGP L3VPN's have two basic mechanisms for controlling connectivity within a L3VPN.

text_preview:
MP-BGP based L3VPNs support flexible connectivity models and are highly scalable, dealing with transport connectivity requirements in 5G environments. They have two basic mechanisms for controlling connectivity: 

1. MP-BGP routing protocol 
2. VPN routing and remote access (VPNRA)

trace: Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Service Models for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Slicing Phase 1 --> Backhaul user plane network \(N3 and N9\)

text: • Virtual Routing and Forwarding \(VRF\) instances: These are local routing table associated with L3VPNs on Provider Edge \(PE\) TNEs. The VRF holds local and remote VPN routing information. Local routes are those learnt by the PE and normally consist of attachment circuits, routes learnt via routing protocols running over attachment circuits or via local static routing. Remote VPN routes are those learnt from remote PEs. They are conveyed between PEs using MP-BGP and held in the PE's BGP table. Installation of remote routes into the VRF routing table is determined by local policies. One of the key policy attributes used to determine what routes are installed into a VRF are Route Targets \(RTs\).

text:
* Three discrete VRFs associated with the phase 1 slices are created on PEs supporting slices. Alphabetic VRF names have been used in the illustration. In reality, VRF names could also be numeric values.
  * o VRF1: MBB o VRF2: MMTC o VRF3: NB-IOT
  * Mobile components associated with each slice connects to the PE via a VLAN attachment circuit which is placed into the appropriate slice VRF.
  * Each VRF on the PE learns local IP subnets containing the mobile slice components, either as connected routes, via a routing protocol or via static routes.
  * A single RT is associated with each slice type. Alphabetic RT names have been used in the illustration. In reality, RT values are numeric values.
  * o VRF1: RT = MBB o VRF2: RT = MMTC o VRF3: RT = NB-IOT
  * Routes from each slice's VRF are exported where they are learnt with their associated RT.
  * On remote PEs each VRF imports the RT associated with their slice.
  * This creates an any-to-any transport network allowing connectivity between all mobile backhaul components in the slice.

text: The data network or N6 is not part of the RAN and is not in scope of the WG-1 slicing work item. However, transport slicing needs to extend to the N6 data network, particularly as the Data Network \(N6\) network extends closer to the radio infrastructure with multiple breakout points and although not discussed in this annex, the techniques outlined for the backhaul and midhaul user plane slicing are largely applicable when building the data networks across a common packet switched transport infrastructure. An important consideration when utilising multiple breakout points in the data network \(N6\) is to ensure traffic exits the network in the desired place but also returning traffic enters the data network \(N6\) in desired place. This requires UPF address block planning within the data network, how these routes are advertised externally by the routers at the peering points and how external routes are advertised within the Data network \(N6\).

text: Transport QoS considerations in a 5G environment
trace: Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Service Models for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Transport Network Quality of Service architecture --> Transport QoS considerations in a 5G environment
text_preview: Transport QoS considerations in a 5G environment

text:
* Section 7 outlines the 5G interfaces the transport network needs to support. In many areas the transport QoS requirements for 5G are very similar to existing 4G and general multi-service environments. However, there are some notable considerations and exceptions.
  * In the context of packet-based switching technologies for O-RAN and 3GPP, the interplay of QoS and transport slicing has two dimensions: 1\) The QoS requirements of O-RAN fronthaul traffic 2\) The QoS requirements of the mobile services, which depends on the kind of application being delivered to the end users. The transport slicing and QoS architectures needs to consider both dimensions to properly allocate QoS resources capable of satisfying the expected requirements for each kind of traffic in terms of bandwidth, latency, etc.
  * O-RAN 7.2X Fronthaul Traffic: The user and control traffic stream is eCPRI based and runs between the O-RU and the O-DU. It is a new traffic type associated with 5G. The transport requirements of the Fronthaul user and control plane interfaces are contained in the O- RAN.WG9.CTRP-REQ-V01.00 \[20\] but can be summarised as high bandwidth and more importantly from a QoS perspective, extremely low delay \(micro-seconds\) traffic. Due to the low delay requirements this traffic type will only ever be seen in the access network and requires packet switching equipment to treat this traffic with the highest priority through the device and when scheduling onto attached interfaces. Today, many Service Providers use the highest priority queue for voice traffic, consequently, changes to the existing QoS schemes may be required.
  * 5G introduces Midhaul: Midhaul interfaces run between the O-DUs and the O-CUs and between O-CUs. The F1 interfaces are a new set of interfaces associated with 5G, but use GTP-U and GTP-C which is the same packet types used in Backhaul. It is expected that Midhaul and Backhaul interfaces will have similar QoS requirements.
  * 5G introduces new service types, each with their own QoS requirements. GTPv1-U \[5\] is used in the Midhaul and Backhaul for F1-U, Xn-U, N3 and N9 interfaces. The importance of user data packet within the mobile environment is indicated in the QoS Field Identifier \(QFI\)Error\! Reference source not found. in the GTP-U extension header\[5\]. High performance TNEs do not have the capability to examine the QFI field and instead use the DSCP field in the IP header or the MPLS Traffic Class to understand the QoS requirements of packets in the transport network. For the transport network to be able to treat GTP-U packets in an appropriate fashion for the mobile service, the Midhaul \(starting from O-RAN slicing phase 2\) and Backhaul \(starting from O-RAN slicing phase 1\) mobile components \(O-DUs, O-CU-UP and UPFs\) must have mechanisms to set a DSCP value in the GTP IP header appropriate to the QoS requirements of the mobile service carried in the GTP-U packet. This could be achieved using a mapping mechanism on the Midhaul and Backhaul mobile components that map QFI values to DSCP values.

text: 3GPP QoS flows and Transport QoS
trace: Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Service Models for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> 3GPP QoS flows and Transport QoS
text_preview: 3GPP QoS flows and Transport QoS

text: The concept of QoS in 4G LTE is based on bearers, while the concept of QoS in 5G mobile systems is based on the QoS Flow concept \[1\] which provides finer granularity. Flows in 5G and 4G bearers can be divided into guaranteed bit rate flows \(GBR QoS flows\) and non-guaranteed bit rate flows \(non-GBR QoS flows\). 5G also has a new delay critical GBR flow category which is not present in LTE. QoS flows also have a service expectation which is expressed in terms of packet delay budget and packet error rate. The mobile QoS requirements are designated through the QoS Class Identifier \(QCI\) in LTE \[2\] and the 5G QoS Identifier \(5QI\) in 5G \[2\]. These identifiers can be operator defined but there is also a standardized list contained in \[1\]. Within the mobile domain traffic \(of flows in 5G or bearers in LTE\) with a given QCI or 5QI should receive the same forwarding treatment \(e.g, in terms of scheduling, admission threshold, etc\)

text:
* Slice traffic above guaranteed rate and below maximum rate: conditionally accepted at the transport edge. Such traffic is marked at the transport edge with QoS marking \(DSCP or MPLS Traffic Class bits\) representing high drop probability. Using Class based Weighted Random Early Discard \(CBWRED\) functionality, described in Annex D: Quality of Service , and implemented on transit Transport Network Equipments, when the transit links are nearing the congestion \(transmit queues on transit links are building up\) CBWRED kicks in, and starts to drop packets marked with QoS marking representing high drop probability. Thus, when no congestion is observed in the transport network, slice traffic can go up to the contracted value \(no drop at the transport edge for traffic volumes below slice maximum rate\), but when congestion is close, high drop probability packets \(above guaranteed rate but below maximum rate\) are being dropped at transit. This ingress marking behaviour at the transport edge can be implemented with 2-rate 3-color policer.
  * Slice traffic above maximum rate \(or above guaranteed rate, if maximum rate is not specified during slice creation/modification\): unconditionally dropped at the transport edge. This behaviour can be implemented with 1-rate policer \(when slice guaranteed rate equals to maximum rate\), or 2-rate 3-color policer \(when different guaranteed and maximum rates are specified for the slice\)

text: 1 Core QoS
trace: Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Service Models for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> 3GPP QoS flows and Transport QoS --> 1 Core QoS
text_preview: 1 Core QoS

text: Transport core QoS is based on a flat model with 4 to 8 queues. Transport core QoS settings are rather static in the nature, provisioned at the time the transport network infrastructure \(interface settings, IGP settings, BGP settings, etc.\) is provisioned. Especially, there is no direct correlation between transport core QoS and 5G slices being created/modified/deleted. Transport core QoS doesn't maintain any state related to individual 5G slice, neither adjust its QoS parameters based on 5G slices creation/modification/deletion events.
trace: Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Service Models for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> 3GPP QoS flows and Transport QoS --> 1 Core QoS
text_preview: Transport core QoS is based on a flat model with 4-8 queues. Its settings are static and provisioned at network infrastructure setup. There's no direct correlation between transport core QoS and 5G slice creation/modification/deletion. It doesn't maintain state or adjust QoS parameters based on these events.

text: The goal of transport core QoS is to ensure right prioritization of transport core traffic classes during congestion events caused by network failures and subsequent traffic rerouting, so that during such congestion events traffic classes requiring low latency are using priority forwarding, and traffic classes requiring low drop are not dropped. The goal of transport core QoS is not end-to-end bandwidth management or providing granular guarantees per each 5G slice.
trace: Underlay network for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> Service Models for WG-1 slicing phase 1, 2 and 3 --> 3GPP QoS flows and Transport QoS --> 1 Core QoS
text_preview: The goal of transport core QoS is to ensure prioritization of transport core traffic classes during congestion events caused by network failures and rerouting, so that low-latency traffic uses priority forwarding and low-drop traffic isn't dropped. This aims to prevent end-to-end bandwidth management or granular guarantees per 5G slice.

With high weight parameterization this queue behaves almost as priority queue.

text: To avoid starvation of the remaining queues during congestion events, priority queue, as well as highly over dimensioned bandwidth queue must have a policer or shaper to limit the rate \(PIR – Peak Information Rate\) of the queue. Queue buffer sizes in both cases must be aligned to maximum latency requirements of the traffic assigned to the queue.

text: Figure 26-20 outlines an example of queue assignment on hardware platforms supporting multiple priority queues, dequeued in strict priority order. With multiple priority queues available it is recommended to place PTP packets in unaware mode in the highest priority queue, to minimize the PDV of these packets to the highest possible degree. Putting these packets above CPRI\(RoE\) or eCPRI has only minimal influence on CPRI/eCPRI packets PDV, since PTP packets are very small \(~100 bytes\). For example, serialization delay of such small packet on 10 GE interface is only 80 ns, so PDV factor contributing to CPRI/eCPRI PDV is very small as well and can be easily handled by the CPRI/eCPRI reassembly functions.
